chapters.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Three thousand years ago, the world was still young. The western continent was a vast wilderness, and most of Europe was home to wild, wandering tribes. Only a few nations, at the eastern end of the Mediterranean and in the nearby parts of Asia, had learned to live in cities, to write, to make their own laws, and to lead more orderly lives. The most brilliant of these nations was Greece. Its people were destined to play a great part in the world, in war, learning, government, and the arts, and to become the true founders of our modern civilization. Even while they were still a rough people, they held noble ideals of beauty and courage, of duty and justice. Before they even had writing, their singers were making songs about their heroes and their great deeds. Fathers taught these songs to their children, and those children taught them to theirs, until at last the songs were gathered into two long and wonderful poems. Those poems have delighted the world ever since: the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_.

The _Iliad_ tells the story of the siege of Ilium, also called Troy, on the western coast of Asia Minor. Paris, the son of the king of Troy, had lured Helen away from her husband’s home. She was the most beautiful woman in Greece, and the wife of a Greek king. To win her back, the kings and princes of the Greeks gathered an army and a fleet and sailed across the Aegean Sea. For ten years they struggled to take the city. In the fine old legends, the gods themselves joined the war, some taking the side of the Greeks and some the side of the Trojans. In the end the Greeks captured the city thanks to Ulysses, a famous Greek warrior who was as brave and fierce as he was wise and crafty.

The second poem, the _Odyssey_, tells what happened to Ulysses, whom the Greeks also called Odysseus, on his journey home. He sailed from Troy with his little fleet. The ships were so small that they used oars as well as sails. He was fated to wander for ten more years before he could get back to his rocky island of Ithaca, on the west coast of Greece, and to his faithful wife, Penelope.

His adventures were marvelous, because the gods who had stood against the Greeks at Troy had plotted to bring him bad luck. His ships were just rounding the southern cape of Greece, safe so far, when a fierce storm swept them off course and carried them to many strange lands. These were lands of giants, man-eating monsters, and wondrous enchantments, which you will enjoy reading about. The determined wanderer fought his way through countless dangers. He lost ship after ship from his little fleet, and companion after companion from his own crew, until he reached home alone and without a friend. There he found his palace, his property, and his family all in the power of a band of greedy princes. He defeated them with his cunning and his strength, and his long trials were over.

As you read these ancient tales, you must set aside what you know about the world and see it the way the Greeks did. They knew only a small part of it, the eastern end of the Mediterranean, yet even that seemed to them a great and marvelous region. Beyond its borders lay strange and mysterious lands full of wonders of every kind, and around it all flowed the great world-river, the encircling stream of Ocean.

The gods lived on the mountains of Olympus, to the north. There was Zeus, the greatest of all, god of thunder and the wide sky; Hera, his wife; Apollo, the archer god; Athene, the wise and clever goddess; Poseidon, who ruled the sea; Aphrodite, goddess of love; Hephaestus, the skilled craftsman; Ares, god of war; Hermes, the swift messenger; and others as well, whom you will come to know as you read. People worshipped all of them with prayers and sacrifices. As in the early legends of many peoples, the gods often took the shape of men and women. They had favorites and they had enemies, and they ruled the fates of mortals as they pleased.

If you let yourself be drawn into this old, simple way of seeing earth and heaven, you will not only love these ancient tales yourself, but you will also see why, century after century, they have been loved longer and better than any other tales, by old and young, by men, women, and children alike. For they are hero-tales: tales of war and adventure, of courage and nobility, of the heroes whom people have looked up to, almost since the beginning of time, as models of wisdom, strength, and beauty.
THE ODYSSEY

chapters.title: The Counsel of Athene
paragraphs: When the great city of Troy had fallen, all the chiefs who had fought against it set sail for home. But the heavens were angry with them, and they did not have a safe and happy journey. One was shipwrecked. Another was shamefully killed in his own palace by his unfaithful wife. Others found everything at home troubled and changed, and were forced to look for new homes elsewhere. Some were driven far and wide around the world before they saw their native land again. Of them all, the wise Ulysses[1] wandered farthest and suffered most. Ten years were almost over, and he was still far away from Ithaca[2], his kingdom.

The gods had gathered in council in the hall of Olympus[3], all except Poseidon,[4] the god of the sea, who had gone to feast with the Ethiopians. Poseidon hated Ulysses more than any of them, and he was the one keeping him from his home.

Then Athene spoke among the immortal gods. “My heart aches for Ulysses. He is suffering terribly on an island in the sea, where the daughter of Atlas holds him and tries to make him forget his native land. He longs[5] to see even the smoke rising from the land where he was born, and he wishes he were dead. And you pay no attention at all. Didn’t he offer you many sacrifices in the land of Troy? Why are you so angry with him?” Zeus, the father of the gods, answered her. “What are you saying, my daughter? It is Poseidon who is so angry with Ulysses, because he blinded Poseidon’s son Polyphemus[6] the Cyclops.[7] But come, let us make a plan together so that Ulysses can return to his home. Poseidon will not be able to stand against all of us.”

Then Athene said, “If that is your will, let us send Hermes[8], the messenger, to Calypso’s[9] island, to tell the goddess that we have decided Ulysses shall go home. And I will go to Ithaca and stir up the spirit of his son Telemachus[10]. First he will speak his mind to the suitors who are courting his mother and wasting his wealth.[11] Then he will go to Sparta and to Pylos[12] to ask for news of his father. In this way the young man will earn a good name among men.”
So she went to Ithaca, where she took the form of Mentes[13], the chief of the Taphians.[14]

Many princes from the islands had gathered in the house of Ulysses. They were suitors of Queen Penelope[15], because they said Ulysses was dead and she ought to choose another husband. There they sat, playing checkers[16] and feasting. Telemachus sat among them, sick at heart, because they were wasting his property and he was not master in his own house. But when he saw the guest at the door, he got up from his seat, welcomed him, and made him sit down. He ordered food and wine to be brought for him. When the guest had finished eating, Telemachus asked what had brought him there.

Then the false Mentes said, “My name is Mentes, and I am king of the Taphians. I am sailing to Cyprus to get copper, and I am trading iron for it. I have been a friend of this house for a long time, to your father and to your father’s father. I came hoping to see your father, because I was told he was here. But now I see that some god has held back his return, since I know very well that he is still alive. But tell me, who are these people I see? Is this a gathering of a clan, or a wedding feast?”

Telemachus answered, “Sir, while my father was alive, our house was rich and respected. But now that he is gone, things are not going well for me. I would not grieve so much if he had fallen in battle before Troy. Then the Greeks would have built him a great burial mound, and he would have won lasting fame, which would have passed to his son as well. But instead the storms of the sea have swept him away, and I am left in terrible distress. The men you see here are the princes of the islands, and they come to court my mother. She neither refuses nor accepts, and meanwhile they sit here and eat up my property.”

Then the false Mentes said, “May the gods help you! You badly need Ulysses. But now listen to my advice. First, call an assembly of the people. Tell the suitors to go back, each one to his own home. As for your mother, if she wants to marry, let her go back to her father’s house, so that her relatives can prepare a wedding feast and the gifts a well-loved daughter should have. After that, fit out a ship with twenty oars and go to ask about your father. Perhaps someone will give you news of him, or perhaps you will hear a voice from Zeus about him. Go to Pylos first, and then to Sparta, where Menelaus lives, the last of all the Greeks to come home. If you hear that your father is dead, then come back here, raise a mound for him, and give your mother to a new husband. And when you have done all this, plan how you can kill the suitors, by force or by trickery, for it is time for you to think like a man.”

Then Telemachus said, “You speak out of a friendly heart, the way a father would speak to his son, and I will never forget your words. But now I beg you to stay here a little while, so that I can give you a fine gift, the kind friends give one another, to be an heirloom in your family.”
But the false Mentes said, “Don’t keep me any longer, for I am eager to leave. Give me your gift when I come back.”
Then the goddess left, and as she flew away she looked like a sea eagle. Telemachus knew, as she went, that she was a goddess.
Meanwhile the minstrel Phemius[18] was singing to the suitors, and his song was about the unhappy homecoming of the Greeks from Troy.

When Penelope heard the song, she came down from the upper room where she had been sitting, with two handmaids keeping her company. When she reached the place where the suitors sat, she stood by the doorway of the hall and held her shining veil in front of her face. Weeping, she spoke to the minstrel. “Phemius, you know many songs about the deeds of gods and men. Sing one of those, and let the guests drink their wine in silence. But stop this pitiful song, for it breaks my heart to hear it. Surely I am the unhappiest of all women, for the husband I mourn was so famous.”

But Telemachus answered her. “Mother, why do you begrudge the minstrel for pleasing us in the way his spirit moves him? It is no fault of his that he sings of the Greeks’ unhappy homecoming. People value most the song that sounds newest to their ears. So bear it and listen, for Ulysses was not the only one who never came home. Many other famous chiefs never made it home either. Go back to your room and look after your household, and tell your maids to get on with their work. Speech belongs to men, and most of all to me, the master of this house.”
Then she went back to her room, amazed at her son, because he had spoken with such authority. There she wept for her husband, until Athene sent sleep down upon her eyes.

When she had gone, Telemachus spoke to the suitors. “Let us feast now and be merry, and let there be no fighting among us. It is good to listen to a minstrel whose voice is like the voice of a god. But in the morning let us go to the assembly, where I will say plainly what I want: that you leave this hall and eat your own food. But if you think it better to eat up another man’s goods and pay nothing back, then go ahead. But Zeus will certainly make you pay.”

So he spoke, and they were all amazed that he dared to be so bold. Then Antinous[19] answered, “Telemachus, surely it is the gods who have taught you to speak so boldly. So I pray that Zeus never makes you king in Ithaca.”

Then Telemachus said, “It is no bad thing to be a king. His house grows rich, and he himself is honored. But there are others in Ithaca, young and old, who could have the kingship now that Ulysses is dead. Still, know this: I will be lord of my own house, and of the slaves that Ulysses won for himself with his own spear.”

Then Eurymachus[20] spoke. “It is for the gods to say who will be king in Ithaca. But no one can deny that you should keep your own goods and be lord in your own house. Tell me, who is this stranger who came to your house just now? Did he bring news of your father? Or did he come on some business of his own? He left in a strange way, and he did not stay long enough for us to get to know him.”
Telemachus answered, “Truly, Eurymachus, the day of my father’s return is gone forever. As for this stranger, he said he was Mentes, king of the Taphians.”
So Telemachus spoke, but in his heart he knew that the stranger was Athene. Then the suitors turned to dancing and singing, and they made merry until dark. After that, each one went home to sleep.

But Telemachus went to his room, thinking over many things in his heart. Eurycleia,[21] who had nursed him when he was small, went with him, carrying torches in her hands. He opened the door of the room, took off his tunic, and put it into the wise woman’s hands. She folded it, smoothed it, and hung it on a peg. Then she left the room, pulled the door shut, and fastened it. And all night long Telemachus thought in his heart about the journey Athene had shown him.

chapters.title: The Assembly
paragraphs: When morning came, Telemachus told the heralds to call the people to the assembly. The heralds called them, and they came quickly. When they had gathered, he walked to the meeting place, holding a spear in his hand, with two dogs following him. Then Athene poured a marvelous grace over him, so that everyone stared at him in wonder as he sat down in his father’s seat.

The first to speak was Aegyptus[1], a man bent with age and very wise. He had four sons. One had sailed with Ulysses to Troy, one was among the Queen’s suitors, and two stayed at home with their father to work the farm. He said: “Listen to me, men of Ithaca! No assembly has met in Ithaca since Ulysses went away. Who has called us together now? If it was Telemachus, what does he want? Has he had news that the army is coming home? I think he is an honest man. May Zeus be with him and give him what he hopes for!”
The old man finished, and Telemachus was pleased with his words. He stood up and said:—

“My heart is heavy, men of Ithaca. First, my father, whom you all loved, is dead. And now the princes of the islands keep coming to our house to court my mother, though she is still waiting for her husband to come home. They are eating us out of everything we own. Ulysses is not here to protect it, and I truly am not strong enough. It is a terrible wrong, and I cannot bear it.”
Then he threw his scepter on the ground and sat down in tears. Antinous, one of the suitors, got up and said:—

“No, Telemachus, don’t blame us. Blame your mother, who is more cunning than any woman alive. This is the fourth year we have been coming to ask for her hand, and all this time she has fooled us with false hopes. Listen to what she did. She set up a great loom and said to us: ‘Suitors of mine, listen. Don’t rush my marriage until I finish this web. It is to be a burial cloth for Laertes[2], the father of Ulysses, because it would be a shameful thing if a man who owned so much went without this honor.’ That is what she told us. For three years she tricked us, because whatever she wove by day she unraveled at night. But when the fourth year came, one of her maids told us the secret. We came upon her at night and caught her unraveling what she had woven during the day. Then she had to finish it, very much against her will. So send your mother away, and tell her to marry whomever she likes. Until that is done, we won’t leave.”
Telemachus replied: “How can I send away against her will the woman who gave birth to me and raised me? I can’t do it.”

As he finished speaking, two eagles appeared. They flew side by side until they were over the assembly. There they circled in the air, shook many feathers loose from their wings, tore at each other, and flew off.

Then the prophet Alitherses[3] cried out: “Be warned, suitors! Great trouble is coming for you, and for others too. As for Ulysses, I said when he left for Troy that he would return after twenty years, and so he will.”

The suitors would not listen, and Telemachus said: “Give me a ship and twenty rowers, so that I can go to Pylos and Sparta. Perhaps I will hear some news of my father. If I learn that he is dead, I will come back here, build a mound for him, and give my mother to a new husband.”

With that he sat down. Then Mentor[4], the man Ulysses had put in charge of his household when he left, stood up in the middle of the crowd and said: “From now on, no king should ever be kind and gentle at heart or try to do what is right. Let him be harsh and unjust instead. Not one person among the people he ruled remembers Ulysses now, and yet he was as gentle as a father. If the suitors want to do evil, I won’t stop them. They do it at the risk of their own necks. My anger is with the people, who sit there speechless and don’t shout shame on the suitors. There are many of you, and the suitors are few.”

Leocritus[5], one of the suitors, answered: “Mentor, you must be out of your mind to tell the people to put us down. In truth, if Ulysses himself came back and tried to drive the suitors out of the hall, it would go badly for him. He would meet a terrible end if he fought them. As for the people, they should go home. Let Mentor help the young man on his voyage, since he is a friend of the family. Still, I doubt he will ever make it.”
With that, the assembly broke up.

Telemachus went off alone to the seashore. He washed his hands in the sea and prayed to Athene: “Hear me, you who came to our house yesterday and told me to take a ship and sail across the sea to look for news of my father! The people are holding up my plan, and the suitors are stirring them up with their wicked hearts.”

While he was praying, Athene came and stood beside him. She looked and sounded like Mentor. She said: “You have spirit, and you will surely turn out to be a true son of Ulysses and Penelope. So I have good hope that the journey you speak of won’t be for nothing. As for the suitors, don’t think about them. They talk nonsense, and they don’t know that their doom is already close. Go and speak with the suitors as before, and get supplies ready for the journey, wine and meal. I will gather men who will volunteer to go, and I will find a ship too, the best in Ithaca.”

Telemachus went back to the house. In the courtyard the suitors were skinning goats and singeing pigs. Antinous grabbed him by the hand and said, “Eat and drink, Telemachus, and we will find you a ship and rowers, so you can go wherever you like to ask about your father.”

But Telemachus answered: “Do you think I will eat and drink with you, when you waste my property so shamefully? Be sure of this: I will take revenge on you. And if you refuse me a ship, I will go in somebody else’s.”
With that he pulled his hand out of Antinous’s grasp.
Another suitor said, “Now Telemachus will go and find help against us in Pylos or Sparta. Or maybe he will put poison in our cups and kill us all.”
Another said: “Maybe he will die too, the way his father did. Then we could divide up everything he owns. We would give the house to his mother and her new husband.”

So they jeered at him. But he went to his father’s storeroom, where many casks of old wine were lined up, along with gold, bronze, clothing and olive oil. The careful Eurycleia, who kept the house, looked after all these things. He said to her: “Nurse, get twelve jars of wine ready for me. Not the best, but the next best. And twenty measures of barley meal. I will take them in the evening, when my mother is asleep, because I am going to Pylos and Sparta. Perhaps I will hear some news of my father.”

The old woman began to cry. “What are you thinking, my only son, going abroad like this? Do you want to die the way your father did? This evil pack of suitors will plot to kill you and divide your property. You had better stay quietly at home.”
Telemachus said: “I go because the gods tell me to. Just swear that you won’t say a word to my mother until eleven or twelve days have passed, unless she happens to ask about me.”

The old woman swore that it would be so. Telemachus went back among the suitors. Meanwhile Athene had taken his shape and gathered a crew, and she had also borrowed a ship for the voyage. To keep the suitors from getting in the way, she made a deep sleep fall on them, so that they dozed where they sat. Then she came to the palace in the form of Mentor and called Telemachus out, saying:
“The rowers are ready. Let’s go.”

Athene led the way, and they found the ship’s crew on the shore. Telemachus spoke to them: “Come, friends, let’s carry the food aboard. It is all in the storeroom, and no one knows about it. Not my mother, not any of the maids, only one woman.”
So the crew went to the house with him, carried all the supplies down, and stowed them in the ship. Then Telemachus climbed aboard and sat at the stern, and Athene sat beside him.

When he called to the crew, they got ready to leave. They lifted the pine mast, set it in its socket, and fastened it with ropes. Then they hauled up the white sails with straps of ox-hide. The wind filled the sail, and the water foamed around the front of the ship as she rushed through the sea. When everything on board was fastened down, they filled the mixing bowl with wine and poured offerings to the gods, above all to Zeus.
All night long, until dawn, the ship raced across the sea.

chapters.title: Nestor’s Tale
paragraphs: At sunrise the ship reached Pylos, where Nestor lived. It happened that the people were holding a great sacrifice on the shore for Poseidon. There were nine groups, with five hundred men in each, and nine bulls for every group of five hundred. They had tasted the inner parts and were burning slices of meat on the thigh-bones for the god when Telemachus and his crew tied up the ship and stepped onto the shore. Athene said to Telemachus: “You have no need to be ashamed now. You have crossed the sea to hear news of your father. Go to Nestor and find out what he has in the depths of his mind.”
But Telemachus answered, “How can I speak to him, when I am so young and have no experience?”
“You can,” said the goddess. “You will think of something yourself, and the gods will put something into your mouth.”

With these words she led the way, and they came to where Nestor sat with his sons and a great crowd around him, getting the feast ready. When the people saw the strangers, they took them by the hands and sat them down on soft fleeces. Nestor’s son Peisistratus[1] brought them food and wine in a golden cup. He gave the wine to Athene first, since he thought she was the older of the two. He said, “Please pray to Lord Poseidon and pour your drink offering. When you have done that, hand the cup to your friend so that he can do the same.”
Athene took the cup and prayed to Poseidon: “Give glory to Nestor and his son, and reward the men of Pylos for this great sacrifice. And let us accomplish what we have come here to do.”
The son of Ulysses prayed in the same way.
When they had eaten and drunk as much as they wanted, Nestor said: “Strangers, who are you? Do you sail the seas to trade, or are you pirates, roaming about and risking your lives?”

Telemachus answered, with Athene putting courage into his heart: “We come from Ithaca, and our business is our own. I am looking for news of my father, who long ago fought at your side and helped sack the city of Troy. We have heard about all the others who fought the Trojans, whether they returned or where they died. But the death of this one man is still a mystery. That is why I have come to you. Perhaps you will be willing to tell me about him, whether you saw him die with your own eyes or heard of it from someone else. Don’t soften your words out of pity for me. Tell me plainly what you saw.”

Nestor answered: “You remind me of everything we went through, fighting around Priam’s great city. The best of us were killed there. Brave Ajax[2] lies there, and Achilles[3], and Patroclus[4], and my own dear son. Who could tell the whole story of what we suffered? No one could, not if you stayed here five or six years to listen. For nine whole years we were busy planning the enemy’s ruin, and Zeus still did not bring it about. In cunning Ulysses always beat the rest of us, your father Ulysses, if you really are his son. And truly, you speak like him. You would not think a younger man could sound so much like an older one. But listen to my story. When we had sacked the town, I sailed home across the sea at once and left the others behind. So I do not know for myself which of the Greeks were saved and which were lost. But don’t you wander far from home, my son, while strangers eat up your property. Go to Menelaus, who has only recently come back from a distant country. Go and ask him to tell you everything he knows. If you like, go with your ships. Or if you prefer, I will send you in a chariot with horses, and my sons will be your guides.”
Then Athene said: “Let’s cut up the tongues of the animals, mix the wine, and pour offerings to Poseidon and the other gods. Then we should think about sleep, because it is time.”

She finished, and they listened to her. When the offerings were done, Athene and Telemachus got ready to go back to their ship. But Nestor stopped them. He said: “May Zeus and all the gods forbid that you should leave my house for your ship, as if I were a poor man with no rugs or blankets in his house for his guests to sleep on! Not so. I have rugs and blankets enough. As long as I am alive, and my children after me, the son of my friend Ulysses will never lie down on a ship’s deck. We will entertain strangers in my hall.”

The false Mentor said: “That is kind of you, dear father. Let Telemachus stay with you. I will go back to the ship, cheer up the crew, and tell them everything. I will sleep there tonight, and tomorrow I go to the Cauconians[5], where I am owed a debt that is neither small nor new. But you should send this young man on his way in your chariot.”
Then the goddess left in the form of a sea-eagle, and everyone who saw it was amazed.

“You will be no coward or weakling, since the gods attend you even now in your youth. That was none other than Athene, the daughter of Zeus, the same goddess who stood by your father in the land of Troy.”

After this, the old man led the whole company to his house. There he mixed them a bowl of wine that was eleven years old. They prayed to Athene, and afterward they lay down to sleep. Telemachus slept on a bed under the gallery, with Peisistratus beside him.

The next day, as soon as it was morning, Nestor and his sons got up. The old man said: “One man should go to the plain for a heifer, and another to the ship of Telemachus to tell the whole crew to come here, leaving only two behind. A third should order the goldsmith to cover the heifer’s horns with gold, and the maids should get everything ready for a feast.”
They did as the old man ordered. After they had offered the sacrifice and eaten and drunk, old Nestor said, “Now harness the horses to the chariot, so that Telemachus can be on his way.”

The men harnessed the horses, and the housekeeper loaded the chariot with food and wine and the fine delicacies that princes eat. Peisistratus took the reins, and Telemachus rode beside him. They traveled all that day, and when darkness fell they reached the city of Pherae[6] and spent the night there. The next day they set out again and arrived at Lacedaemon[7], at the palace of King Menelaus.

chapters.title: In Sparta
paragraphs: As it happened, Menelaus was holding a great feast that day. His daughter, the child of the lovely Helen, was marrying the son of Achilles, to whom she had been promised back at Troy, and his own son was taking a wife as well. The two travelers stopped their chariot at the gate, and the steward saw them. He went to Menelaus and said:—
“Look, my lord, two strangers have arrived, and they look like the sons of kings. Should we keep them here, or send them on to someone else?”

Menelaus was angry. “Have we ourselves not eaten so often at other men’s tables?” he said. “Are we now to send these strangers elsewhere? No. Unharness their horses and bring them in to dinner.” So the servants unhitched the horses, tied them in the stable, and gave them grain, and they led the two men into the hall. The visitors stared in wonder, for the palace of Menelaus shone like the sun or the moon. When they had looked their fill, they bathed in the polished baths. Then they took their seats beside Menelaus. A maid brought water in a golden pitcher and poured it over a silver basin so that they could wash their hands. She pulled up a polished table next to them, and a housekeeper set out food, laying many delicacies on the board. A carver served them platters of meat and placed golden cups beside them.
Then Menelaus said: “Eat and enjoy yourselves. When you have finished, I will ask who you are, for you look like the sons of kings.”
When the meal was over, Telemachus looked around the hall and said to his friend:—
“Look at all the gold and amber, the silver and ivory. This must be what the hall of Zeus is like.”
He said this in a whisper, with his mouth close to his friend’s ear, but Menelaus overheard and said:—

“No mortal house can compare with the homes of the gods. Still, among men there may be some who own things as fine as these. I have wandered far and gathered many treasures in many lands. But alas for me! I wish I had only a third of this wealth, if only the men who died at Troy were alive again. Most of all I grieve for the great Ulysses, for no one knows whether he is living or dead.”

At the mention of his father, Telemachus began to cry and held his purple cloak up over his eyes. Menelaus saw it and understood who he was. He wondered whether to wait until the young man spoke of his father himself, or to ask him first why he had come. While he was still thinking it over, the lovely Helen came in with three maids. One set out a chair for her to sit on, one spread a rug for her feet, and one carried a basket of purple wool, while Helen herself held a golden distaff in her hand. When she saw the strangers, she said:—

“Who are these men, Menelaus? I have never seen anyone, man or woman, who looks so much like Ulysses as this young man does. It must be his son Telemachus, the baby he left at home when you all went to Troy for my sake!”

Menelaus answered: “It must be so, my lady. He has the hands and feet of Ulysses, and the same eyes and hair. And just now, when I said Ulysses’ name, he wept and held his cloak in front of his face.”
Then Peisistratus said: “King Menelaus, you are right. This is the son of Ulysses, and he has come to you. Perhaps you can help him with advice or with action.”

Menelaus replied: “Then he is the son of a man I loved dearly. I meant to bring him here from Ithaca with all his belongings and give him a city of his own in this land. Then nothing but death itself would ever have parted us. But the gods have arranged it differently.”

At these words they all began to weep: the lovely Helen, Telemachus, and Menelaus. Even Peisistratus could not hold back his tears, for he was thinking of his dear brother, who had been killed at Troy.
Then Menelaus said: “Let us stop crying now. Tomorrow Telemachus and I have much to say to each other.”

Then the lovely Helen dropped a powerful drug into the wine they were drinking. It is called nepenthe[1]. It is so strong that anyone who drinks it will not weep for the whole day, even if his father and mother die, or if men kill his brother or son before his eyes.

After that, Helen said: “It would take a long time to tell of all the clever and brave things Ulysses did. But you should hear one of them. While the Greeks were camped outside Troy, he disguised himself as a beggar and slipped into the city. He had even beaten himself many times, so that he looked as if he had been cruelly abused. I was the only one who recognized him, and I questioned him, but he gave me slippery answers. I swore that I would not give him away. So he killed many Trojans with his sword and learned many things. And while the other women of Troy wailed, I was glad, for my heart had turned back toward home.”

Then Menelaus said: “What you say is true, my lady. I have met many men and traveled through many lands, but I have never seen anyone who could match Ulysses. I remember well when the other Greek chiefs and I sat hidden inside the wooden horse, and you came to it. Some god who favored the Trojans must have put the idea in your heart. Three times you walked around our hiding place and called out to each of the chiefs by name, and you sounded remarkably like his wife. We wanted to jump up from where we sat, or answer you right away. But Ulysses held us back, and in this way he saved all the Greeks.”
But Telemachus said: “None of that has saved him, though. He is dead.”
After that, they went to sleep.
[1] ne-pen’-the

chapters.title: Menelaus’s Tale
paragraphs: The next day Menelaus asked Telemachus: “For what purpose have you come here to lovely Lacedaemon?”

Telemachus answered: “I came to ask whether you can tell me anything about my father. Some men who want to marry my mother are eating up my property, and I see no one to help me. So tell me honestly: do you know anything about my father yourself, or have you heard news of him from someone else?”
And Menelaus replied:—

“I was held up for a long time at the river AEgyptus, though I was desperate to get home. The gods kept me there because I had not made them the proper sacrifices. Now, out in the surging waves off the coast of Egypt there is an island called Pharos[1]. It lies a full day’s sail from the land, if the wind blows steadily at a ship’s back. The gods kept me there for twenty days, and the sea winds never rose. My food would have run out, and my men would have died, if the daughter of Proteus[2] had not taken pity on me. She felt sorry for me when she found me wandering alone, away from my crew, who were all roaming the island and fishing with hooks because they were so hungry. She came up to me and said: ‘Are you a fool, stranger, or weak in the head? Or are you sitting around on purpose, because you enjoy suffering? You have been here a long time and cannot find a way out, while your men lose heart.’ I answered: ‘I will tell you the truth, whoever you are. I am not staying here by choice. I must have sinned against the gods. Tell me, which of the gods have I offended, and how can I find a way to get home?’ At once the goddess replied: ‘I will tell you everything. My father Proteus, who knows the depths of the whole sea, comes to this place. If you can ambush him and catch him, he will show you the way and tell you how to cross the water home.’ I answered: ‘Help me plan this ambush, so that he does not see me first and escape, because it is hard for a man to overpower a god.’ Then the goddess said: ‘When the sun has climbed to the middle of the sky, the old man comes up out of the sea. He comes on the breath of the west wind, hidden under the ripples. When he has come ashore, he lies down to sleep in the caves, and all around him sleep the seals, the sea’s own herd, and they breathe out the bitter smell of salt water. At daybreak I will lead you there, you and three of your companions. Choose the bravest men you have from your ships. Now I will tell you the old man’s habits. First he will count the seals, and then he will lie down in the middle of them, like a shepherd among his flock. As soon as you see him lying there, remember your courage, and hold him down. He will take the shapes of every creature that crawls on the earth, and of water, and of blazing fire. But grip him tightly and press him hard. When he turns back into his own shape, let him go, and ask him which of the gods is angry with you and how you can get back across the sea.’ With that she dived beneath the waves, and I went back to the ships, deeply troubled. The next morning I took the three comrades I trusted most. And there she was, having brought up from the sea the skins of four sea-calves, freshly skinned, for she meant to trap her own father. She dug hiding places for us in the sand and made us lie down in them, and she threw a sea-calf’s skin over each of us. It would have been a dreadful ambush, because the stench of the skins nearly sickened us. (Who would want to lie down beside a sea beast?) But she rescued us. She took some ambrosia[3], which smells very sweet, and put it under each man’s nose to cancel out the stink of the animal.

“So we waited all morning, steady-hearted. The seals came up out of the water and lined up along the shore. At noon the old man came out of the sea and walked along the row of sea beasts, counting them. He counted us among them, too, and did not notice the trick. Then he lay down to sleep. We rushed at him with a shout and held him tight. He did not forget his cunning, though. He turned into a bearded lion, then a snake, then a leopard, then a huge wild boar. He also took the shape of running water and of a flowering tree. All the while we held on to him. When at last he was tired, he said: ‘Son of Atreus[4], which of the gods told you to ambush me like this?’ But I answered: ‘Old man, why do you try to fool me with twisted words? I am stuck on this island and can find no way off it. Tell me which of the gods is holding me back, and how I can get home across the sea.’ The old man answered: ‘Before you set out, you should have offered a sacrifice to Zeus and the other gods, if you wanted to reach your own country quickly. Now you must go back to the river AEgyptus and make offerings to the gods. Then they will give you what you want.’ My spirit sank when I heard that I had to make that long, weary trip again. But I said: ‘Old man, I will do everything you say. But tell me, please: did the other Greeks, whom Nestor and I left behind at Troy, get safely home? Or did some of them die a terrible death on their ships or among their friends?’ The old man replied: ‘You are making a mistake to ask such things, for you will weep to hear them. Your brother escaped the dangers of the sea, but the storm wind carried him to the land where Aegisthus lived. When Agamemnon[5] set foot on his own soil, he kissed it and wept hot tears, he was so glad to see it again. But Aegisthus set an ambush for him and killed him and all his companions.’ Then I wept bitterly and did not care to live any longer. But the old man said: ‘Do not weep, son of Atreus, for tears will not help. Hurry home instead, so that you can take revenge on AEgisthus.’[6] His words comforted my heart, and I said: ‘There is one more man I would like to hear about. Is he still alive, wandering on the sea, or is he dead? Tell me, even if it hurts me to hear.’ The old man answered at once: ‘You mean the son of Laertes. I saw him on an island, in the home of Calypso. He was shedding great tears, because the nymph is keeping him there by force. He cannot get back to his own country, for he has neither a ship nor companions.’ So Proteus spoke, and plunged into the sea. The next day we went back to the river AEgyptus, the stream that is fed by heaven, and sacrificed to the gods. I also built a great burial mound for my brother Agamemnon, so that his name would not be forgotten among men. When all this had been done properly, I set sail and came back to my own country, for the gods gave me a fair wind. But now stay with me in my halls. When you want to leave, I will give you a chariot with three horses, and a fine cup as well, from which you can pour offerings to the gods.”

Telemachus answered him: “Do not keep me long, son of Atreus. My companions are waiting for me in Pylos, though I would be happy to stay with you for a whole year without ever feeling homesick. And I hope whatever gift you give me is something I can treasure. But I will not take horses to Ithaca. Let them stay here and decorate your home, for you rule a wide plain with wheat and rye and barley. In Ithaca there is no meadow land. It is a country for goats, and yet it is dearer to my eyes than any fine pasture for horses could be.”

Then Menelaus said: “You speak well, as the son of your father should. Come, I will change the gifts. From all the treasures in my house I will give you the finest, especially a bowl that the King of the Sidonians gave me. It is made of silver, and its rim is finished in gold.”

Meanwhile, word had reached the suitors in Ithaca that Telemachus had gone on this journey to look for his father, and they were very displeased. After talking it over, they decided the best plan was to set an ambush for him and kill him on his way back home. So Antinous took twenty men and set out, planning to lie in wait in the strait between Ithaca and Samos.[7]

Penelope knew of this plot too, because the herald Medon[8] had overheard it and told her that Telemachus had gone to look for news of his father, and that the suitors planned to kill him on his way home. She called in her maidservants, young and old, and scolded them. “That was a wicked thing to do,” she said. “You knew he was about to leave, and not one of you woke me. If I had known, I would have kept him here, however eager he was to go!”

Then Eurycleia answered, “Put me to death if you like, but I won’t hide anything from you. I knew what he meant to do, and I gave him what he needed for the journey. He made me swear not to tell you until the eleventh or twelfth day had passed. Now go with your maidens and pray to Athene to save him from death. The gods do not hate this house altogether.”

So Penelope, having prepared herself properly, went up to the upper room with her maidens and prayed aloud to Athene to save her son. The suitors heard her praying and said to one another, “The Queen must be praying about her wedding. She has no idea that her son is about to die.”

Then she lay down and fell asleep, and while she slept Athene sent her a dream that looked like her own sister. The vision stood above her head and said, “Are you sleeping, Penelope? The gods don’t want you to grieve, because your son will certainly come home.”

Penelope replied, “How did you get here, sister? You live so far away. And how can I stop weeping when my husband is lost? Now my son has gone too, and I am terribly afraid for him, in case his enemies kill him.”
But the vision answered, “Don’t be afraid. He has a powerful helper with him, Athene herself, and she has told me to bring you this message.”
Penelope said, “If you are a goddess, then tell me this. Is my husband still alive?”
The vision replied, “That I cannot tell you, whether he is alive or dead.” With these words it faded into the air.
When Penelope awoke, she felt calm and comforted at heart.
[1] Pha’-ros.
[2] Pro’-teus.
[3] ambrosia: the food of the gods.
[4] A’-treus.
[5] Ag-a-mem’-non.
[6] AE-gis’-thus.
[7] Sa’-mos.
[8] Me’-don.

chapters.title: Ulysses on his Raft
paragraphs: Once again the gods sat in council on high Olympus, and Athene spoke to them.

“Let no king ever bother to act justly,” she said, “because no one remembers Ulysses, who was like a father to his people. He is far away, a prisoner on Calypso’s island, with no ship to carry him back to his own country. Meanwhile the suitors are determined to kill his son, who has gone to Pylos and Lacedaemon to find news of his father.”

Zeus answered her, “What are you saying? Didn’t you plan all this yourself, so that Ulysses could take his revenge on the suitors? As for Telemachus, guide him with your skill, as you well can, so that he reaches his own land unharmed and the suitors’ work is wasted.”
Then he turned to Hermes. “Hermes, go to the nymph Calypso and tell her my firm decision: Ulysses is to go home now.”

So Hermes put on his golden sandals, took his wand in his hand, and came to the island of Ogygia[1] and the cave where Calypso lived. It was a lovely place. A fire of sweet-smelling wood burned in the cave, and Calypso sat at her loom, singing in a beautiful voice. Around the cave stood a grove of alders, poplars and cypresses, where many birds, falcons and owls and sea crows, liked to roost. A vine with purple clusters of grapes grew all around the cave’s mouth, and four fountains ran in four different directions through meadows of parsley and violets. The place was so beautiful that even a god would marvel at it, and Hermes stood there marveling. Then he went into the cave, and Calypso recognized him the moment she saw him face to face, for the gods know one another even when their homes are far apart. But Ulysses was not there. As usual, he was sitting on the seashore, weeping and groaning, because he could not see his wife and home and country.

Calypso said to Hermes, “Why have you come here, Hermes of the golden wand? You are welcome, but it has been a long time since you visited me. Tell me everything you have in mind, and I will do it if I can. But first come with me, so I can set out some food for you.”
She laid a table with ambrosia and put it beside him, and she mixed the red nectar[2] for him, and the messenger ate and drank. When he had refreshed himself with food, he said:—

“You ask why I have come, and I will tell you the truth. I did not come because I wanted to. Who would choose to cross such a wide sea, where there is no city of men who offer sacrifices to the gods? Zeus ordered me to come, and no one can go against the orders of Zeus. He says you are keeping a man who has suffered more than all his companions, the men who fought at Troy for nine years and set out for home in the tenth. All the rest of his company were lost, but the waves carried him to your island. Now send him home as quickly as you can, because it is not his fate to die far from his friends. He will see the high roof of his house again, and his own country.”
This upset Calypso very much, for she would gladly have kept Ulysses with her forever. She said:—

“You gods are always jealous when a goddess loves a mortal man. And as for Ulysses, didn’t I save him when Zeus struck his ship with a thunderbolt and all his comrades died? Well, let him go, if that is what Zeus wants. But I can’t send him myself, because I have no ship and no rowers. Still, I will gladly teach him how to get home safely.”
Hermes said, “Do it quickly, or Zeus will be angry with you.”

Then he left. Calypso went looking for Ulysses and found him on the seashore, gazing out over the water and weeping. He was tired of living, so badly did he long to see Ithaca again. She stood beside him and said:—

“Don’t grieve for your native country, and don’t waste away with tears. If you want to go, I will help you on your way. Take your axe, cut some beams, fasten them together and build a deck on top. I will give you bread, water and wine, and clothes as well, so that you can get back safely to your own country, for the gods have willed it.”

“No,” said Ulysses, “what are you saying? Am I to cross the dreadful sea on a raft, where even ships don’t pass without damage? I won’t go against your wishes, but first you must swear the great oath of the gods that you are plotting no harm against me.”

Calypso smiled and said, “What strange words. I swear that I plan no harm against you, only the good I would want for myself if I were in need. My heart is not made of iron, you know. It is full of compassion.”
Then the two of them went to the cave and sat down to eat. She set before him the food that mortal men eat, while she herself ate ambrosia and drank nectar. Afterward she said:—

“Why are you so eager to get home? If you knew all the trouble waiting for you, you wouldn’t go. You would stay here with me instead. And though you long all day to see your wife, I am surely just as beautiful as she is.”

“Don’t be angry,” Ulysses replied. “Wise Penelope can’t be compared with you, of course, since she is a mortal woman and you are a goddess. Still, my home is dear to me, and I long to see it again. And if some god wrecks me on the open sea, I will bear that too with a patient heart. I have already suffered a great deal, and worked hard through the dangers of war and the dangers of the sea. Whatever is still to come, let it be added to what has already happened.”

The next day Calypso gave him an axe with an olive-wood handle and an adze, and led him to the far end of the island, where great trees stood, long dead and dry: alder, poplar and pine. He cut down twenty of them, trimmed off the branches and shaped the trunks to a straight line. Then the goddess brought him an auger, and he drilled holes in the logs and joined them with pegs. He also built decks and side planking, a mast and a yard, and a rudder to steer the raft. He fenced it all around with a rail of willow twigs to keep out the waves. Calypso wove the sails, and Ulysses fitted them with braces, halyards and sheets. Last of all, he pushed the raft down into the sea with levers.

By the fourth day everything was finished, and on the fifth day he set out. Calypso gave him fine clothes, a skin of wine, a skin of water, and plenty of food in a leather bag. She also sent a fair wind blowing from behind, and Ulysses set his sails and went happily on his way. He did not sleep but watched the stars, the Pleiades[3] and Bootes[4], and the Bear, which always turns in the same place, keeping watch on Orion.[5] For Calypso had told him, “Keep the Bear always on your left as you cross the sea.”

He sailed for seventeen days, and on the eighteenth the shadowy hills of the island of the Phaeacians[6] came into view. But now Poseidon, on his way back from feasting with the Ethiopians, spotted him sailing, and it made him furious. He shook his head and said to himself, “So the gods must have changed their minds about Ulysses while I was away among the Ethiopians. Now he is close to the island of the Phaeacians, and if he reaches it he will escape his misery. Even so, I will send him far enough along a road of trouble first.”
With that he gathered the clouds and stirred up the deep, holding his trident in his hand. He raised a storm of every wind that blows and covered land and sea with clouds.

Ulysses was deeply troubled, and said to himself, “Calypso told me the truth when she said I would suffer many troubles on my way home. I wish I had died the day the men of Troy hurled so many spears around the dead Achilles. Then the Greeks would have buried me. Now I am going to die a miserable death.”

As he spoke, a huge wave struck the raft and flung him far off, and the rudder fell from his hand. For a long time he could not rise, he sank so deep, weighed down by the fine clothes Calypso had given him. But at last he surfaced, spat the salt water out of his mouth, lunged for the raft, caught hold of it and sat on it, carried this way and that by the waves. But Ino[7] saw him and pitied him. She had once been a woman and was now a goddess of the sea. She rose from the deep like a seagull on the wing, perched on the raft, and said:—

“Unlucky man, why does Poseidon hate you so? He will not kill you, much as he wants to. Take off those clothes and swim for the land of Phaeacia, with this veil tied under your chest. When you reach the land, untie it, and throw it into the sea.”

Then the goddess gave him the veil and dived back into the deep, the way a seagull dives, and the waves closed over her. Ulysses thought it over and said to himself, “Oh, no! Can it be that another god is setting a trap for me, telling me to leave my raft? I certainly won’t take her advice yet, because when I saw the land it looked a long way off. I know what I’ll do. As long as the raft holds together, I will stay on it, and when the waves break it apart, then I will swim, for there is nothing better to be done.”

But while he was thinking this, Poseidon sent another huge wave against the raft. As a stormy wind scatters a heap of husks, so the wave scattered the timbers of the raft. But Ulysses straddled one beam, the way a man sits on a horse. He pulled off the fine clothes Calypso had given him, tied the veil under his chest, and jumped into the sea, stretching out his arms to swim.
When Poseidon saw him, he shook his head and said, “Go on wandering over the sea, then, until you reach the land. You won’t be able to say you haven’t had trouble enough.”
But Athene held back the other winds and roused the swift north wind, so that Ulysses could escape death.

So he swam for two days and two nights. On the third day the sea was calm, and from the top of a great wave he saw land close by, though the waves were still high. But as he came nearer he heard the surf breaking along the shore, for there was no harbor there, only cliffs and jagged rocks.

At last his knees went weak with fear, and his heart melted inside him. Heavy-spirited, he spoke to himself: “Oh, no! Beyond all hope Zeus has let me see land, and now there is no place where I can get out of the sea onto the shore. The crags are sharp, the waves roar around them, the smooth rock rises straight up from the water, and the sea is deep, so I can’t find a foothold. If I try to land, a great wave may smash me on the rocks. If I swim along the shore to look for a harbor, I’m afraid the winds will catch me again and carry me out into the deep. Or some god may send a sea monster against me, and there are certainly plenty of them out in the sea pastures, and I know Poseidon is furious with me.”

While he was weighing all this in his heart, a great wave carried him toward the rocks. His skin would have been torn off and all his bones broken, if Athene had not put a thought into his heart. He rushed in toward the shore, grabbed the rock with both hands, and clung to it until the wave had passed. But as it flowed back, it caught him and dragged him out into the deep again. Just as a cuttlefish is pulled out of its hole in the rock, so he was dragged away by the water, and the skin was torn from his hand against the rocks. Ulysses would have died then, if Athene had not put a plan in his heart. He swam outside the breakers, along the coast, looking for a spot where the waves might be broken, or a harbor. At last he came to a place where a river ran into the sea. It was free of rocks and sheltered from the wind, and Ulysses felt the current of the river as he went. Then he prayed to the river-god:—
“Hear me, O King, whoever you are. I have come to you, running from the anger of Poseidon. Save me, O King.”

At that, the river held back its current and smoothed the water in front of Ulysses, so that he finally made it to dry land. His knees buckled, his arms hung limp, and salt water poured out of his mouth and nose. He was out of breath and could not speak. When he had recovered, he untied the veil from under his chest and threw it into the salt current of the river. The stream carried it out to sea, and Ino rose up and caught it in her hands.

Then he lay down among the reeds on the riverbank and kissed the ground. He thought to himself, “What am I going to do now? If I sleep here by the river, I’m afraid the dew and the frost will kill me, because the wind off the river blows cold in the early morning. But if I go up into the woods and lie down to sleep in the thicket, I’m afraid some wild beast will eat me.”

In the end, the woods seemed the better choice, so he went. They were close to the river, and there he found two bushes, one a wild olive and the other a cultivated olive. They grew so thickly tangled together that no wind could blow through them, no sun could pierce them, and no rain could get in. Ulysses crept underneath and found a huge heap of leaves, enough to shelter two or three people even in winter, when the rain falls hard. Ulysses was glad. He lay down in the middle and covered himself with leaves. Then Athene poured deep sleep over his eyelids, to ease him after all his hardship.
[1] O-gyg’-i-a.
[2] nectar: the drink of the gods.
[3] Plei’-a-des.
[4] Bo-o’-tes.
[5] O-ri’-on.
[6] Phae-a’- ci-ans.

chapters.title: Nausicaa
paragraphs: Meanwhile Athene went to the city of the Phaeacians, to the palace of their king, Alcinous[1]. She made her way to the bedroom where Nausicaa, the king’s daughter, lay asleep, a girl as lovely as a goddess. Athene stood over her in the form of a girl her own age, a friend she was fond of.

Athene said, “Nausicaa, how did your mother end up with such a careless daughter? Look, your clothes are lying there unwashed, and your wedding day is coming soon. You will need good clothes for yourself, and some to give to those who will lead you to your bridegroom’s house, because that is how a bride earns respect. So get up at dawn and go wash the clothes, and I will go with you. First thing in the morning, ask your father to give you mules and a wagon to carry the clothes and robes. It is also more fitting for you to ride than to walk, because the washing places are a long way from the city.”

When morning came, Nausicaa woke up, still wondering about her dream, and went to look for her parents. She found her mother with her maids at the loom, spinning yarn dyed sea-purple, and she met her father on his way to a council with the leaders of the land. She said to him, “Father, please give me the wagon and the mules, so I can take the clothes down to the river and wash them. You should always have clean robes when you go to council, and I also have five brothers who like to have freshly washed clothes when they go dancing.”

She said nothing about her own marriage. But her father understood what she was thinking, and he answered, “I won’t refuse you the mules or anything else, dear child. My men will get a wagon ready for you, with strong wheels and a frame on top.”

He called to his men, and they prepared the wagon and harnessed the mules. The girl carried the clothes out of her room and loaded them in. Her mother packed a basket with all kinds of food and filled a goatskin bottle with wine. She also gave her olive oil, so that Nausicaa and her maids could rub themselves with it after bathing. Nausicaa took the reins and flicked the mules with the whip. Hoofs clattered, and the mules trotted off with their load and never grew tired.

When they reached the river, where there was plenty of water for washing clothes, the girls unhitched the mules from the wagon and turned them loose to graze on the sweet clover along the bank. Then they took the clothes out of the wagon, carried them to the water, and stamped on them in the washing pits. When all the clothes were clean, they spread them out on the shore, where the waves had rinsed the pebbles spotless. After that they bathed and rubbed themselves with oil, and then sat down by the river to eat and drink. When the meal was over, they played ball and sang while they played, with Nausicaa leading the song. She was the loveliest of all the girls. When the game was over and they were hitching up the mules and folding the clothes, Athene arranged things so that the princess threw the ball to one of her maids and sent it far off course, into the river. All the girls screamed, and Ulysses woke up. He said to himself, “What country have I come to? Are the people here cruel, or kind to strangers? Just now I thought I heard the voices of nymphs[2]. Or am I near the homes of men?”

He twisted a leafy branch around his waist, got up, and walked toward the girls. They were terrified at the sight of him, since he looked like a wild man, and they ran off in every direction. But Nausicaa stood her ground. Then Ulysses called out:—

“O Queen, I cannot tell whether you are a goddess. But if you are a mortal, your father and mother are fortunate, your brothers too, and the luckiest of all is the man who wins you as his bride. I have never seen a man or woman so beautiful. You remind me of a young palm tree that I recently saw growing beside the god’s temple. As for me, I was washed up on this shore after leaving the island of Ogygia. Have pity on me, then. Lead me to the city, and give me something to wrap around myself, even a piece of this linen. May the gods give you every blessing!”

Nausicaa replied, “Stranger, you seem to be neither wicked nor foolish. You will not go without clothes or food, and I will take you to the city. You should also know that this country is Phaeacia, and I am the daughter of its king, Alcinous.”

Then she called to her maids, “Why do you run away just because you see a man? No enemy is coming here to hurt us. The gods love us, and we live on an island in the sea, so no one can reach us to do us harm. If a man arrives here worn down by trouble, it is right to help him. So give this man food and drink, and wash him in the river, where the wind can’t reach.”

So they led him down to the river and gave him clothes, along with olive oil in a golden flask. At his request they moved a little way off, and he washed the salt from his skin and hair, rubbed himself with oil, and put on the clothes. Athene made him taller and handsomer, and gave him thick hair the color of a hyacinth. Then he sat down on the beach, wonderful to look at, and the girl said:—

“This man has not come to our land without the gods’ will. At first I thought he looked rough, but now he looks like one of the gods. I would be quite happy to have a husband like him, and perhaps he would like to stay here. Maids, give him food and drink.”
They did, and he ate greedily, having gone hungry for a long time. Then Nausicaa ordered the mules hitched up and said to Ulysses:—

“Stranger, get up and come with me, and I will take you to my father’s house. But do as I tell you. While we are passing through the fields, follow quickly with the maids behind the wagon. But when we reach the city—you will see a high wall, and a harbor on each side of the narrow road that leads to the gate—stop following the wagon. Close to the wall is a grove of poplars sacred to Athene, with a spring in the middle and a meadow all around it. Wait there until I have reached my father’s house. I don’t want people to gossip about me. I’m sure that if you were with me, someone would say, ‘Who is this tall, handsome stranger with Nausicaa? Will he be her husband? Maybe he is a god who came down because she prayed for him, or a man from far away, since she looks down on the men of Phaeacia.’ It would be shameful for people to say such things. So when you think I have arrived at the palace, go up and ask for my father’s house. Anyone can show you, even a child, because none of the other Phaeacians live in a house like it. Once you are inside the doors, go quickly through the hall to where my mother sits. Her seat is close to the hearth, and my father’s is right beside it, where he sits sipping his wine like a god. Pass him by, kneel before my mother, and beg her to give you a safe return to your own country.”

Then she struck the mules with the whip. They quickly left the river behind, but the girl took care to drive at a pace that Ulysses and the maids could keep up with on foot. At sunset they came to Athene’s sacred grove. There Ulysses sat down and prayed to Athene: “Hear me now, daughter of Zeus, and let these people look on me with pity.”
So he prayed, and Athene heard him, but she did not show herself to him face to face, because she feared the anger of her uncle Poseidon.
[1] Al-cin’-o-us.
[2] nymphs: spirits of the woods and waters

chapters.title: Alcinous
paragraphs: Nausicaa arrived at her father’s house. Her brothers unhitched the mules from the wagon and carried the clothes inside, and she went up to her room, where a nurse lit a fire for her and made her a meal.

At the same time Ulysses set out for the city. Athene wrapped him in a mist, because she did not want any of the Phaeacians to see him and make fun of him. Just as he was about to enter the city, the goddess took the shape of a young girl carrying a pitcher, and met him.
Ulysses asked her, “My child, could you please tell me where Alcinous lives? I am a stranger in this place.”
She answered, “I will show you, because he lives near my own father. But keep quiet, since we Phaeacians don’t care much for strangers.”

Then Athene led the way and Ulysses followed. As he went, he marveled at the harbors, the ships, the meeting places, and the walls. When they reached the palace, Athene said, “This is the place you asked about. Go in. You will find kings at dinner here, but don’t be afraid, because a fearless man always does best. And look first for Queen Arete.[1] If she is kindly disposed toward you, you will surely see your own country again.”
With those words Athene left, and Ulysses went into the palace. It shone with a glow like the sun or the moon.

It was an amazing place. The walls were bronze, and the golden doors hung on silver posts. On either side of the door stood dogs of gold and silver. Seats lined the wall all the way from the threshold to the inner room, and on them sat the Phaeacian chiefs, feasting. Golden statues of youths stood holding torches to light up the darkness. Fifty women worked in the house, grinding grain and weaving cloth, since the women of that land are as skilled at weaving as the men are at sailing. All around the house were beautiful gardens with orchards of figs, apples, pears, pomegranates, and olives. Neither drought nor frost harmed them, and one harvest followed another without a break. There was also a vineyard, where some grapes were drying in the sun, some were being picked, and others were just starting to turn red. There were flower beds of every kind, and in the middle of it all were two springs that never ran dry.

Ulysses looked at all this for a while, then walked into the hall. The Phaeacian chiefs were there, drinking their last cup in honor of Hermes. He passed quickly through them and clasped the knees of Arete. As he spoke, the mist lifted from around him, and everyone in the hall saw him:—
“I beg you, and your husband, and your guests: send me home to my own country. May the gods bless you and them, and may you live in peace, and may your children inherit that peace after you!”
Then he sat down in the ashes of the hearth. For a while everyone was silent, but at last Echeneus[2], the oldest man in the land, spoke:—

“King Alcinous, it isn’t right for this man to sit in the ashes of your hearth. Lift him up and have him sit on a chair. Let us pour an offering to Father Zeus, who is the friend of strangers, and have the housekeeper give him food and drink.”

Alcinous did so, telling his eldest son, Laodamas[3], to give up his seat. An attendant poured water over the stranger’s hands, and the housekeeper gave him food and drink. When everyone had poured out an offering to Father Zeus, King Alcinous said, “Tomorrow morning we will call the people to an assembly and discuss how to take this stranger home, so that he arrives without trouble or pain. We will bring him home unharmed, but what happens to him there we cannot know. That will be as the Fates spun his thread. But if he is a god and not a man, then this is some new scheme of the gods. Until now they have always appeared to us openly, when we offer sacrifices, and they sit beside us at our feasts. Even if a traveler meets them on the road, they don’t disguise themselves, since they are close kin to us.”

Then Ulysses spoke: “Don’t think such thoughts, O King! I am no god. I am the most miserable of all human beings. I could tell of many sorrows. Still, let me eat, because however sad a man may be, he must eat and drink. When day comes, get ready and take me to my home. I would gladly die if I could only see my home again!”
They agreed that it would be done, and each went home. Only Ulysses was left in the hall, with Alcinous and Arete. Arete recognized his clothes, and said:—
“Where are you from, stranger? And who gave you these clothes?”
Ulysses then explained that he had left the island of Calypso, told her all he had been through, and described how Nausicaa had come upon him on the shore and shown him the way to the city.

Alcinous blamed the girl for not bringing him to the house herself. “No,” said Ulysses, “she would have brought me, but I refused, because I was afraid of your anger.” He said this because he did not want the girl to be blamed.

Alcinous replied, “I’m not angry over something like that. I would gladly have a man like you as my son-in-law, and I would give him a house and riches. But I won’t keep anyone here against his will. As for sending you home, that’s easy. Lie down and sleep, and my men will strike the sea with their oars and carry you wherever you wish, even to the farthest country in the world. My ships are truly the best that sail the sea, and my young men are the most skillful rowers there are.”
When Ulysses heard these words, he was glad. And within himself he prayed, “Father Zeus, let Alcinous fulfill everything he has said, and let me reach my own land!”

Then Arete ordered her maids to prepare a bed for the stranger. They left the hall with torches in their hands and got it ready. When they had finished, they called Ulysses and said, “Get up, stranger, and go to sleep. Your bed is ready.”
He was very glad to sleep, after all he had been through.
[1] A-re’-te.
[2] E-che-ne’- us.
[3] La-o’-da-mas.

chapters.title: The Phaeacians
paragraphs: At dawn the next day the King got up, and so did Ulysses, and the King led the way to the meeting place. In the meantime Athene took the form of the King’s herald and went through the city. To every man she said, “Come to the assembly, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians, and hear about the stranger who has just arrived at the palace of Alcinous.”

In this way she stirred up their curiosity, and the meeting place was packed full. The men stared in wonder at Ulysses, because Athene had poured a marvelous grace over him, making him look taller, stronger and handsomer than before.

Then the King stood and spoke. “Listen, captains and counselors of the people, to what I have to say. This stranger has come to my palace. I don’t know who he is or where he comes from, whether from the east or the west, but he asks to be taken safely home. So let us choose a ship that has never been to sea, and fifty-two young men who are the best rowers. When you have made the ship ready, come to my house and feast, for I will provide well for everyone. Call Demodocus[1] the minstrel too, because the gods have given him, more than anyone, the gift of song to delight people’s hearts.”

They did as the King advised. They prepared the ship and moored it by the shore, and then they went to the King’s palace. It was crowded from one end to the other, with young and old alike. Alcinous killed twelve sheep, eight pigs and two oxen for them, and his men prepared a splendid feast for the people.

Then the King’s servants came in, leading the blind minstrel by the hand. They seated him in a silver chair in the middle of the guests, hung a harp above his head, and showed him how to reach up and take it. Beside him they set a table with a basket and a cup of wine, so that he could drink whenever he liked.

So the Phaeacians feasted in the hall, and when they had eaten and drunk enough, the minstrel began to sing. His song, whose fame had reached the heavens, was about the quarrel between Ulysses and Achilles during the fighting to take Troy.

As the minstrel sang, Ulysses held his purple cloak over his face, because he was ashamed to be seen weeping in front of everyone. Each time the singer paused, Ulysses wiped away his tears. But the chiefs loved the song, so whenever the minstrel started again, Ulysses covered his face once more and wept. Nobody noticed this except Alcinous.
Then the King said to the chiefs, “Now that we have feasted and enjoyed the music, let us go outside, so that this stranger can see how good we are at boxing, wrestling and running.”
Many Phaeacian young men stood up. The handsomest and strongest of them was Laodamas, the King’s eldest son. They ran races, wrestled, threw quoits and jumped.
Then Laodamas said to Ulysses, “Won’t you try your skill in some game, stranger, and shake the trouble from your heart?”
But Ulysses answered, “Why do you ask me this? My troubles are on my mind more than sports, and all I care about is seeing my home again.”
Another young man said, “And honestly, stranger, you don’t look like a wrestler or a boxer. You look more like a trader who sails the seas to make a profit.”

“That was badly said,” Ulysses replied. “It is true that the gods don’t give every gift to every man, beauty to one and eloquence to another. You are handsome, so handsome that not even a god could improve you, but you speak foolishly. I am not unskilled at these things. In the old days I was among the best, but since then I have suffered much in war and shipwreck. Still, I will test my strength, because your words have angered me.”

Just as he was, still wearing his mantle, he picked up a quoit much heavier than the ones the Phaeacians usually threw, and sent it spinning. It flew through the air so fast that the brave Phaeacians ducked to the ground in fear, and it landed far beyond all the others.

Then Athene, who had taken the form of a Phaeacian man, marked the spot where it fell. She said, “Stranger, even a blind man could find your mark, because it isn’t lost among the others but lies far past them. Take heart in this contest. None of the Phaeacians will beat you.”

Ulysses was glad to see that he had a friend among these people, and he said, “Now match that throw, young men, if you can. I’ll soon send another after it, as far or even farther. And if anyone feels like it, let him get up and compete with me, because I’ll take on any man in Phaeacia at wrestling or boxing, or even running, except Laodamas, since he is my friend. I can shoot a bow, and I can throw a spear as far as other men can shoot an arrow. In a race, though, someone might beat me, because I have been through so much at sea.”

They all stayed silent until the King stood and said, “You have spoken well. But we Phaeacians are not mighty at wrestling or boxing. We are only fast on our feet and skillful at sailing the sea. And we love feasts, dances, the harp, fine clothes and the bath. In these things no one can surpass us.”

Then the King told Demodocus the minstrel to sing again. When he had finished, the King’s two sons danced together, and afterward they played with a ball, tossing it up into the air, as high as the clouds, and catching it with great skill.
After that the King said, “Let each of us give this stranger a mantle, a tunic and a talent of gold.”

Then all the princes brought their gifts. Alcinous said to the Queen, “My lady, bring a chest here, the best one you have, and put a robe and a tunic in it. And I will give our guest a beautiful golden cup of my own, so that he will remember me all his life whenever he pours out offerings to the gods.”
The Queen brought a fine chest from her room and put in it the gifts the princes had given. With her own hands she added a robe and a tunic. Then she said:
“Look at the lid now, and tie a knot in it, so that nobody robs you on the way while you sleep in the ship.”

So Ulysses closed the lid firmly and tied it with a clever knot that Circe had taught him. After that he went to the bath. As he came from the bath, Nausicaa met him at the entrance to the hall and stared at him in wonder, he looked so handsome. She said, “Farewell, stranger. When you get back to your own country, remember me now and then, because you owe me the price of your life.”
Ulysses answered her, “Nausicaa, if Zeus lets me return safely home, I will honor you like a goddess for the rest of my days, because I truly owe you my life.”

Then he went into the hall and sat down beside the King, and the squire came leading the blind minstrel by the hand. Ulysses had cut a generous piece from the chine[2] of a boar that had been set before him, and he said to the squire, “Take this and give it to Demodocus, because people should honor a minstrel.”
So the squire carried the dish over and set it on the minstrel’s knees, and the minstrel’s heart was glad.

When they had all had enough to eat and drink, Ulysses said to the minstrel, “Demodocus, I don’t know whether the gods have taught you, but you sing of all the toil and trouble the Greeks suffered before the great city of Troy as if you had been there yourself. Now sing to us about the Wooden Horse, and how Ulysses planned to have it taken up into the citadel of Troy after filling it with the bravest chiefs. Sing this truly, and I will tell everyone that you really are a minstrel taught by the gods.”

Then the minstrel sang this song. He told how one group of Greeks set fire to their camp, boarded their ships and sailed away, while the other group, Ulysses and his comrades, sat hidden inside the Horse, which the Trojans themselves had dragged into their place of assembly. The people sat all around it, and three plans were put forward. The first was to split the wood open, the second was to drag it to the brow of the hill and throw it down, and the third was to leave it as an offering to the gods. The third plan won, because it was the city’s fate to be destroyed through the Horse.
The minstrel also sang how the chiefs came out of the Horse and went through the city, laying it waste, and he sang much about Ulysses and his brave deeds.
So the minstrel sang, and as Ulysses listened, his heart melted within him and tears ran down his cheeks.

No one in the company noticed this except King Alcinous. The King spoke up, saying, “Listen, princes of the Phaeacians, and let Demodocus stop singing, because ever since he took up the harp this stranger has not stopped weeping. So let the minstrel stop, and let us enjoy ourselves, as we should. Haven’t we gathered to give gifts to this stranger and send him home? And you, stranger, don’t hide anything from us that I am about to ask. Tell us the name your people call you at home, because everyone has a name. Tell us also about your land and your city, so that our ships can set their course to take you there. These ships are not like other men’s ships, which have steersmen and rudders. They have minds of their own and know the cities of all men. They cross the deep wrapped in cloud, and they have no fear of wreck. But my father used to say that Poseidon held a grudge against us because we carry all men safely home, and that one day he would strike one of our ships on its way back from such a trip and turn it into a rock that would loom over our city. But you, stranger, tell us about yourself: where you have wandered, and what cities you have seen, whether cities of wicked people or of people who welcome strangers and fear the gods. Tell us, too, why you wept when you heard the tale of Troy. Did you perhaps have a relative or a friend among those who died at Troy? A wise friend is always like a brother.”
[1] De-mod’-o-cus.
[2] chine, backbone.

chapters.title: The Cyclops
paragraphs: Then Ulysses answered the King. “What should I tell you first, and what last? The gods have laid so many sorrows on me.
