First I will tell you my name, so that you will know it, and so that there may be friendship between us even when I am far away. I am ULYSSES, SON OF LAERTES. I live in Ithaca. Many islands lie around it, but Ithaca is farthest to the west, and the others face the sunrise. Ithaca is very rugged, but it breeds brave men, and truly, nothing is dearer to a man than his own country. The fair goddess Calypso wanted me to stay with her as her husband, but she could not persuade me, because there is nothing a man loves more than his country and his parents. Now I will tell you about all the troubles the gods sent me on my way from Troy.

“The wind that carried me from Troy brought me to Ismarus[1], a city of the Cicones.[2] I sacked it and killed the people who lived there. But the townspeople called for their kinsmen who lived in the mountains, and they overpowered us and drove us back to our ships. Six men from each ship died, but the rest of us escaped.

“Then we sailed on, grieving for our dear comrades, yet glad to have escaped destruction. When we had gone a short way, Zeus sent the north wind against us in a mighty storm, covering both land and sea with clouds, and the ships were driven before it. We lowered the sails and rowed the ships toward land with all our strength. For two days we suffered great distress and sorrow, but on the third, when morning light came, we raised the sails and rested. I would then have reached my own country, but the north wind and the sea pushed me off course. For nine days the wind carried us along.

“On the tenth day we came to the land where the lotus grows. It is a wondrous fruit, for anyone who eats it no longer cares to see his country, wife or children again. The Lotus-eaters, as the people of that land are called, were a kindly folk. They gave some of the sailors the fruit, meaning no harm, only thinking it the best thing they had to offer. When these men had eaten it, they said they would not sail over the sea any more. When I heard this, I ordered their comrades to tie them up and carry them, sadly complaining, to the ships.

“Then the wind died down, so we took to our oars and rowed for many days until we came to the country where the Cyclopes[3] live. About a mile from the shore there was an island, very fair and fertile, but no one lives there or farms the soil. On the island was a harbor where a ship could be safe from all winds, and at the head of the harbor a stream fell from a rock, with whispering alders all around it. The ships sailed safely into this harbor and were hauled up on the beach, and the crews slept beside them, waiting for morning.

“At daybreak we set out across the island, and the Nymphs who live there drove wild goats toward us so that my men would have meat. We fetched our bows and spears from the ships and shot at the herd, and the gods gave us a rich hunt. I had twelve ships in my fleet, and each ship received nine goats as its share, while I took ten for myself.

“We spent the whole day feasting, eating goat meat and drinking the sweet wine we had carried off from the city of the Cicones. All the while we gazed across at the land of the Cyclops, where we could see smoke rising and hear the voices of men and the bleating of sheep and goats. When the sun went down and darkness covered the land, we lay down on the beach and slept.
“The next morning I called my men together and said, ‘Stay here, dear friends. I will take my own ship and my own crew and go find out whether the people on that island are just or unjust.’

“I boarded my ship and ordered my crew to come with me, and so we sailed to the land of the Cyclops. Near the shore stood a cave with laurel trees around its mouth. This was where the Cyclops lived. He lived alone, a lawless creature, and he did not look like a human being at all. He looked more like a wooded mountain peak standing by itself, apart from the others.

“I told the rest of my men to stay and guard the ship, and I chose twelve of the bravest in the crew and set out. I carried a goatskin full of dark red, sweet wine, a gift from the priest of Apollo[4] at Ismarus. It was so precious that no one in his house knew of it except himself and his wife. When they drank it, they mixed twenty measures of water with one of wine, and the fragrance that rose from the cup was wonderfully sweet. Nobody could easily resist it. I filled a large skin with this wine and took it along. I also carried grain in a bag, because something in my heart told me I would need it.

“We went into the cave and decided it belonged to a rich and capable shepherd. Inside there were pens for the lambs and kids, sorted by age, baskets heaped with cheeses, and milk pails full to the brim, lined up along the wall. But the Cyclops himself was out in the pastures. My companions begged me to leave, and to take some cheeses and a few of the lambs and kids with us if I liked. I refused. I wanted to see what kind of host this strange shepherd would be, and, if possible, to receive a gift from him, as strangers have a right to expect. But his arrival was not going to bring my men any joy.

“The Cyclops came home in the evening, a huge giant, very tall, and when we saw him we ran deeper into the cave in terror. On his shoulder he carried an enormous bundle of pine logs for his fire, and he dropped them outside the cave with a great crash. He drove his flocks inside and shut the entrance with a massive rock that twenty wagons or more could not have moved. Then he milked the ewes and all the she-goats. Half the milk he curdled into cheese, and the other half he set aside for his supper. Next he lit a fire with the pine logs, and the flames lit up the whole cave and showed him me and my men.
“‘Who are you?’ shouted Polyphemus[5], for that was the giant’s name. ‘Are you traders or pirates?’

“The sight and the booming voice made me shudder, but I kept my courage and answered: ‘We are not pirates, mighty sir. We are Greeks on our way home from Troy, followers of the great King Agamemnon, whose fame reaches from one end of heaven to the other. We have come to ask for your hospitality, in the name of Zeus, who rewards or punishes hosts and guests depending on whether they treat each other faithfully.’

“‘No,’ said the giant. ‘It is pointless to talk to me about Zeus and the other gods. We Cyclopes pay no attention to gods, because we think we are far better and stronger than they are. But tell me, where did you leave your ship?’
“But I saw what he was thinking when he asked about the ship. He meant to smash it and take away any hope we had of escape. So I answered him cleverly:
“We have no ship. King Poseidon wrecked ours by driving it against a jagged rock on this coast, and we whom you see here are all who escaped from the waves.”

“Polyphemus said nothing. Without another word he snatched up two of my men as easily as a man might pick up puppies, smashed them on the ground, and tore them limb from limb. He ate them, washing them down with great gulps of milk, and left nothing, not even the bones. The rest of us, seeing this terrible deed, could only weep and pray to Zeus for help. When the giant had stuffed his belly with human flesh and milk from his flocks, he lay down among his sheep and fell asleep.

“I debated long in my heart whether to kill the monster while he slept, for I had no doubt that my good sword would reach his heart, big as he was. But a second thought held me back: if I killed him, my men and I would still die a miserable death, since who could move the great rock that blocked the door of the cave? So we waited for morning with grief in our hearts. The monster woke up, milked his flocks, and then grabbed two more men and ate them for his breakfast. After that he went off to the pastures, but he set the great rock over the mouth of the cave, as easily as a man puts the lid on his quiver.

“All that day I thought about the best way to save myself and my companions, and this is the plan I came to. In the cave lay a huge pole of green olive wood, as thick as a ship’s mast, which Polyphemus meant to use as a walking staff once the smoke had dried it. I cut off a length about six feet long, and my men sharpened one end and hardened it in the fire, and then we hid it. In the evening the giant returned and drove his sheep into the cave. This time he did not leave the rams outside as he usually did, but shut them in too. When he had finished his shepherd’s chores, he seized two more of my men, as before, and ate them. After he had finished his supper, I stepped forward with the wineskin in my hand and said:

“‘Drink, Cyclops, now that you have feasted. Drink, and see what precious things we had on our ship. But no one will ever bring you such gifts again, if you treat strangers as cruelly as you have treated us.’

“The Cyclops drank, and he was delighted. He said: ‘Give me more, and tell me your name, stranger, and I will give you a gift, as a host should. This is truly a rare drink. We have vines here too, but they never bear wine like this. It must be what the gods drink in heaven.’
“I handed him the cup again, and he drank. Three times I gave it to him, and three times he drank it down, not knowing what it was or how it would work on his mind.
“Then I said to him: ‘You asked my name, Cyclops. My name is No Man. Now that you know my name, you should give me your gift.’
“And he said: ‘My gift is that I will eat you last of all your companions.’

“As he spoke, he toppled backward in a drunken sleep. I told my men to take heart, for the time of our rescue had come. They pushed the olive stake into the fire until, green as it was, it was ready to burst into flame, and then they drove it into the monster’s eye. He had only one eye, in the middle of his forehead, with the eyebrow beneath it. I stood over it and leaned on the stake with all my weight and twisted it around, the way a man drills through a ship’s timber. The burning wood hissed in the eye, just as red-hot iron hisses in water when a smith tempers steel for a sword.

“The giant sprang up, tore out the stake, and screamed so loudly that all the Cyclopes living on the mountainside heard him and gathered around his cave. They asked: ‘What is wrong with you, Polyphemus, that you make such an uproar in the peaceful night and keep us from sleeping? Is someone stealing your sheep, or trying to kill you by trickery or force?’ And the giant answered: ‘No Man is killing me by trickery.’
“‘Well, then,’ they said, ‘if no man is hurting you, we cannot help you. No one can escape the sickness that great Zeus may send. Pray to our father Poseidon for help.’
“So they spoke, and I laughed to myself, seeing how well the name I had given him had fooled them.

“Then the Cyclops rolled the great stone away from the door of the cave and sat down in the middle of the entrance with his arms stretched out, to feel whether any of the men inside might try to slip out among the sheep.

“For a long time I thought about how my men and I could best escape. At last I hit on a plan that seemed better than all the others, and I thanked Zeus many times that for once the giant had driven the rams into the cave with the rest of the sheep. Since the rams were big and strong, I tied my men underneath their bellies, using the willow twigs the giant used to make his bed. I took one ram and tied a man under it, and set two others beside it, one on each side. That is how I did it for all six, because only six were left of the twelve who had ventured with me from the ship. There was one enormous ram, far bigger than all the others, and I clung to this one myself, gripping its fleece tightly with both hands. Then we all waited for morning. When morning came, the rams rushed out to the pasture, while the giant sat in the doorway and felt the back of each one as it passed, never thinking to check what might be underneath. The great ram went out last. The Cyclops recognized him as he passed, and said:

“‘What is this, leader of the flock? You are never one to lag behind. You have always been the first to run to the pastures and streams in the morning, and the first to return to the fold when evening came, and now you are last of all. Perhaps you are worried about your master’s eye, which some wretch—No Man, they call him—has destroyed. He has not escaped, and I wish you could talk and tell me where he is hiding. I swear I would smash his brains out on the ground and take my revenge on this No Man.’

“With these words he let the ram go out of the cave. When we were out of the giant’s reach, I let go of the ram and untied my men. We hurried to our ship, remembering to drive the sheep ahead of us, and looking back often until we reached the beach. The men who had stayed with the ship were overjoyed to see us. They did not mourn for those who had died, though we all wanted to, because I forbade it, afraid the noise of their weeping would show the giant where we were. Then we all climbed aboard and sat in order on the benches, and struck the sea with our oars and rowed hard to get away from that cursed land as soon as possible. When we had rowed about a hundred yards, far enough that a man on the shore could still hear a voice, I stood up in the ship and shouted:

“‘He was no coward, Cyclops, whose men you so foully killed in your den. You are justly punished, monster, for devouring your guests in your own home. May the gods make you suffer even worse things than these!’

“In his rage the Cyclops broke off the top of a great hill, a huge boulder, and hurled it toward the place where he had heard my voice. It landed right in front of the ship’s bow, and as it sank, a great wave rose and washed the ship back to the shore. I seized a long pole with both hands and pushed the ship away from the land. Then I ordered my men to row, nodding my head, since I did not dare to speak in case the Cyclops learned where we were. They rowed with all their strength.

“When we had gone twice as far as before, I made as if to speak again, but my men tried to stop me. They said: ‘No, my lord, do not make the giant angrier. We were sure we were lost before, when he threw the great rock and washed our ship back to the shore. And if he hears you now, he may still crush our ship and us with it.’
“But I would not listen. I stood up and said: ‘Hear this, Cyclops! If anyone asks who blinded you, tell them it was the warrior Ulysses, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca.’

“The Cyclops answered with a groan: ‘So the old prophecies have come true. Long ago a prophet came to this land and told me that Ulysses would take away my sight. But I expected a great and powerful man who would overcome me by force, and now a weakling has done it, after tricking me with wine.’

“Then the Cyclops raised his hands to Poseidon and prayed: ‘Hear me, Poseidon, if I am truly your son and you are my father. May this Ulysses never reach his home! Or, if the Fates have decreed that he will reach it, may he arrive alone, with all his men lost, and find bitter trouble in his house!’

“When he had finished, he hurled another huge rock, which nearly struck the end of the rudder but missed it by a hair’s breadth. The wave it raised was so big that it carried us across to the other shore.

“So we came to the island of the wild goats, where we found our companions, who had waited a long time for us, terribly afraid we had been lost. I shared out among my crew all the sheep we had taken from the Cyclops. With one voice they all gave me, as my share, the great ram that had carried me out of the cave, and I sacrificed it to Zeus. All that day we feasted merrily on mutton and sweet wine, and when night came, we lay down on the shore and slept.
[1] Is’-ma-rus.
[2] Ci’-co- nes.
[3] Cy-clo’-pes.
[4] A-pol’- lo.
[5] Pol-y-phe’-mus.

chapters.title: Aeolus; the Laestrygons; Circe
paragraphs: “The next morning we set sail. After some time we reached the island where Aeolus lives. It is a floating island, ringed by an unbroken wall of bronze. For a full month the King welcomed me as a friend, and I told him the whole story of what had happened at Troy.

“Then I told him about my voyage and asked for his help. He gave me a bag made from the skin of an ox nine years old, and in it he had tied up every wind that might work against me, since Zeus has made him keeper of the winds, to stir them up or calm them as he pleases. He fastened this ox-hide bag to the deck of the ship with a silver cord, so that not one wind could slip out. But he let a gentle west wind blow, to carry me and my comrades home. It blew for nine days, and by then we were close to Ithaca, our own country. We could even see the men who tended the beacon fires, because the tenth day was nearly dawning.

“But then, by bad luck, I fell asleep, worn out completely, for I had held the steering oar for all nine days and had not trusted it to any of my comrades. While I slept, my comrades, who had been eyeing the great ox-hide with envy, began to talk among themselves.

“‘It is strange how everyone loves and honors this Ulysses wherever he goes,’ they said. ‘Now he is coming home from Troy with plenty of treasure, while we return with empty hands. Let’s see what Aeolus gave him. I’m sure there is a lot of silver and gold in this ox-hide.’

“So they untied the great bag, and look! All the winds burst out and swept us far from our country. I woke up at the uproar and wondered seriously whether I should throw myself into the sea and die. But I held on, thinking it was better to live. I only covered my face and lay still while the ships were driven along by the winds, until we came back to the island of Aeolus. There we landed, drew water, and ate a meal beside our ships. When the meal was over, I took a herald and one of my company and went to the King’s palace. I found him feasting with his wife and children, and I sat down on the threshold. They were amazed to see me and said, ‘What evil power has held you back, so that you never reached your country and home?’
“Then I answered, ‘Don’t blame me, but the wicked plotting of my comrades, and sleep, which overpowered me to my harm. But please help me once more.’
“But he said, ‘Be gone! We cannot help a man the gods hate, and hated by them you surely are.’
“So Aeolus sent me away. Once more we launched our ships and set out, rowing wearily and heavy-hearted.

“We rowed for six days without resting even at night. On the seventh we came to Lamos[1], a city of the Laestrygons, a land where night is as bright as day, so that a man could earn double wages if he could do without sleep. There was a fine harbor, ringed with cliffs and entered by a narrow mouth with great rocks on either side. Inside it there are no waves at all.

“I moored my ship to the rocks outside, but the others sailed into the harbor. Then I sent out two men and a herald, who found a smooth road along which wagons carried timber down from the mountain to the city. There they met a girl, the daughter of the king of that land, and asked her who ruled the country. She pointed out her father’s lofty palace. When they went inside, they saw the girl’s mother, huge as a mountain and horrible to look at, and she immediately called for her husband. The messengers ran back to the ships, but the king let out a great shout, and the giant Laestrygons came crowding around him. They broke huge stones from the cliffs, each one as big as a man could carry, and hurled them at the ships until the ships were smashed. They speared the men like fish and ate them. That was the fate of every ship in the harbor. I alone escaped, because I cut my mooring rope with my sword and ordered my men to row, which they did with a will.

“After a while we reached the island where Circe lives, the daughter of the Sun. For two days and nights we lay on the shore, in great distress and sorrow. On the third day I took my spear and sword and climbed a hill, because I wanted to see what kind of land we had come to. From the top I saw smoke rising from Circe’s palace, which stood in the middle of a wood. I thought for a while about whether to go straight to the palace I had seen, or to go back first to my comrades on the shore. The better plan seemed to be to return to the ship, tell my comrades to eat their midday meal, and then send them out to explore. But as I went down, some god took pity on me and sent a great stag with mighty antlers across my path. It was heading down to the river to drink, since the sun was hot, and I threw my spear and drove it right through the animal. Then I tied its feet together with green twigs and a fathom of rope, hung the beast around my neck, and carried it to the ship, leaning on my spear. It was heavy, and I could not carry it on one shoulder with only one hand free. When I reached the ship, I dropped my load. The men were sitting with their faces covered, they were so sad. But when I told them to cheer up, they looked up and stared in wonder at the great stag. We spent the whole day feasting on venison and sweet wine, and at night we lay down to sleep on the shore. When morning came, I called my comrades together and said, ‘Friends, I don’t know where we are. I only know, from the smoke I saw yesterday from the hill, that someone lives on this island.’

“The men were deeply troubled to hear this, because they thought of the Cyclops and the Laestrygons, and they cried out loud. Then I divided them into two companies. I put Eurylochus[2] in charge of one and took command of the other myself. I shook lots in a helmet to decide who should go and explore the island, and the lot of Eurylochus jumped out. So he set off with twenty-two comrades. In a clearing in the wood they found Circe’s palace. All around it were wolves and lions, but these did not harm the men. They stood up on their hind legs and fawned on them, the way dogs fawn on their master when he comes from dinner, because he brings the scraps they love. Still, the men were afraid. They stood in the porch and heard Circe singing in a lovely voice as she worked at her loom. Then Polites[3], the dearest of all my comrades and the one I trusted most, said, ‘Someone inside is working a great loom and singing in a loud voice. She is either a goddess or a woman. Let’s hurry and call to her.’

“So they called out, and she came out and beckoned them to follow her. In their foolishness they all went, except Eurylochus. She told them to sit down and mixed them a drink of red wine, barley meal, cheese, and honey, along with powerful drugs that make anyone who drinks them forget everything he loves. When they had drunk it, she struck them with her wand. And look! All at once they had the heads, the voices, and the bristles of pigs, though the heart of a man was in them still. Circe shut them in pigsties and gave them acorns to eat.

“But Eurylochus ran back to the ship with news of what had happened to his comrades. For a while he could not say a word, his heart was so full of grief and his eyes so full of tears. At last, after we had asked him many questions, he told us his story.

“At once I slung my silver-studded sword over my shoulder, took my bow as well, and told him to lead me back the way he had gone. But he grabbed me by both hands and begged me, ‘Don’t make me go there against my will. I am sure that you will never come back yourself, and you won’t bring back any of your comrades either. Let us who are left run away and escape death.’ Then I said, ‘Stay here by the ship, eating and drinking, if you want to. But I must go.’
“When I reached the house, I was met by Hermes of the golden wand, the gods’ messenger, who looked like a handsome young man. He said to me:

“‘Have you come to rescue your comrades, who are pigs now in Circe’s house? No, you will never get back yourself. But wait. I will give you a drug that will give you the power to resist all her spells. When she has mixed you a drink and struck you with her wand, rush at her with your sword as if you meant to kill her. When she begs for peace, make her swear the great oath that binds the gods, that she will not harm you.’

“Then Hermes showed me a certain plant, with a black root and a flower as white as milk. The gods call it ‘Moly,’ and it is very hard for a mortal man to find, but for the gods everything is possible.
“Then Hermes left for Olympus, and I went on to the goddess’s palace with a heavy heart. When I got there I stood in the porch and called out, and Circe came, opened the doors, and invited me in.

“She seated me in a great chair, skillfully carved, with a footstool for my feet. Then she gave me a drink in a golden cup, but she had mixed a deadly charm into it. I drank it, but I was not bewitched, because the herb protected me. Then she struck me with her wand and said, ‘Go to the sty now and lie down with your friends.’ At that I drew my sword and rushed at her as though I meant to kill her. She dropped to clasp my knees and cried out, ‘Who are you? What family do you come from? I am amazed that you could drink the potion I enchanted and take no harm. I thought no mortal man could do that. You must have a soul that no enchantment can touch. You must surely be Ulysses, who was to come to this island on his way home from Troy, as Hermes told me. But come, let us be friends.’ Then I said to her, ‘How can we two be friends, goddess, when you have turned my companions into pigs? I fear you have some trick in mind, and that you will catch me off guard and do me great harm. Swear a mighty oath, the oath that binds the gods, that you will not harm me.’
“Then Circe swore the mighty oath, the very oath that binds the gods.

“After this her handmaids, beautiful women born from the springs, the streams, and the woods, prepared a feast. One spread purple covers over the chairs, another brought silver tables up to the chairs and set golden baskets on them. A third mixed sweet wine in a silver bowl and set golden cups beside it, and the fourth filled a great kettle with water and lit a fire under it. When the water boiled, she drew a bath for me, and the bath took the weariness out of my limbs. When I had bathed, a handmaid brought water in a golden pitcher and poured it over a golden basin so that I could wash my hands. Then the housekeeper brought wheat bread and set out many delicacies on the table, and Circe told me to eat. But I sat silent and sorrowful, with other thoughts in my mind.

“When the goddess saw that I was silent and was not eating, she said, ‘Why do you sit there, Ulysses, as if you were mute? Are you afraid of some trick of mine? That cannot be, for haven’t I sworn the great oath that binds the gods?’
“Then I answered, ‘How could anyone think of food and drink after such things have happened to his companions?’

“Circe then walked ahead with her wand in hand, swung open the sty doors, and herded out the pigs who had once been men. She smeared a different strong drug on every one of them. Their bristles dropped away and they were men again, but younger and better-looking than they had been. They saw me, threw their arms around me, and wept for joy, and even Circe felt pity.
“Then she said to me, ‘Go to your ship, Ulysses, and store all your goods and gear in the caves on the shore. Then come back here yourself and bring your comrades with you.’
“So I went. The men who had stayed behind were overjoyed to see me, as glad as calves that have been shut in the farmyard when their mothers come back in the evening.
“So we went to Circe’s home, and she feasted us like kings, and we stayed with her for a whole year, perfectly content.
“But when the year was over, my companions said to me, ‘It is good to remember your country, if the gods truly mean for you to return to it.’
“Then I begged Circe to send me on my way home, as she had in fact promised to do. And she answered:
“‘I would not want you to stay in my house against your will. But first you must make another journey, to the dwellings of the dead, to speak with the seer[4] Teiresias[5].’
“But I was deeply troubled to hear this, and I wept aloud and said, ‘Who will guide us on this journey? No ship has ever made such a voyage as this.’

“Circe answered, ‘Son of Laertes, don’t worry that you have no guide. Just raise the mast, spread the sails, and sit down with your companions, and the north wind will carry you to where you are headed. After you cross the stream of Ocean, you will reach a barren shore with tall poplars and willows growing on it. Beach your ship there, and walk on to the house of Hades.[6] You will find a rock where two rivers meet, the river of fire and the river of wailing. Dig a trench there, a cubit[7] long and a cubit wide. Pour a drink offering for the dead into it, and sprinkle white barley over that. As you do this, call on the dead, and promise that when you come home to Ithaca, you will offer them a barren heifer, the best you have, and that you will sacrifice a black ram, the finest in your flock, to Teiresias alone. When you have finished praying to the dead, offer up a black ram and a black ewe. Then many spirits of the dead will come, but don’t let them drink the blood until you have spoken to Teiresias. The seer will come to you quickly and tell you how to get home.’ The next morning I woke my companions and said, ‘No more sleeping. Let’s be on our way, for Circe has told me everything.’

“So I spoke, and they agreed. Even so, I did not bring my whole crew safely away from the goddess’s house. There was a man named Elpenor[8], the youngest of us all, who was neither brave nor very sensible. He had been sleeping apart from the others on the roof, because he wanted the cool air. When he heard our voices and the tramp of the men’s feet as they moved about, he jumped up suddenly. He forgot to go down by the ladder he had climbed up, and fell straight off the roof. His neck broke, and he went down to the houses of the dead.

“As my men were on their way, I said to them, ‘You think you are going home to your own country. You are not. Circe has shown me a different journey that we must make first, to the house of Hades, so that I can speak with the spirit of Teiresias the seer.’
“So I spoke, and their spirits sank. They sat down right where they were, wept, and tore their hair. But their weeping did them no good.
“Meanwhile Circe had gone ahead and tied a ram and a black ewe to the ship. She slipped past us as we walked, for no one can see the gods who never die when they come and go.”
[1] La’-mos.
[2] Eu- ryl’-o-chus.
[3] Po-li’-tes.
[4] seer, prophet
[5] Tei-re’-si-as
[6] Ha’-des
[7] cubit, a foot and a half
[8] El-pe’-nor.

chapters.title: The Dwellings of the Dead
paragraphs: “After this we got the ship ready to sail, loaded the black sheep aboard, and set off. Circe sent a wind from behind us that filled the sails, and all day long our ship ran swiftly over the sea.

“When the sun went down, we reached the farthest edge of the ocean. I told two of my comrades to prepare the sheep for sacrifice, and I dug a pit a cubit in every direction. Into it I poured a drink offering of honey and milk, then sweet wine, then water, and I sprinkled barley over it all. Next I took the sheep and killed them, so that their blood ran into the trench. The dead gathered to the place: young women, old men worn down by many years of sorrow, and warriors killed in battle, their arms stained with blood. They all crowded around the pit with a terrible cry, and I was badly frightened. I told my comrades to burn the bodies of the sheep and pray to the gods of the dead. I myself sat down beside the pit, and I would not let the souls of the dead come near the blood until I had questioned Teiresias.

“The first to come was the soul of my comrade Elpenor. I was amazed to see him, and I asked, ‘How did you get here, Elpenor, to the land of darkness? How did you get here on foot faster than my ship?’ Elpenor answered, ‘I fell from the roof of Circe’s palace. I forgot about the ladder and broke my neck. But now I beg you, if you love your wife and your father and your son, don’t forget me when you go back to Circe’s island. Burn me with fire, along with my armor, and build a mound for me by the seashore, so that people will hear of me and my fate in years to come. And set my oar on top of my tomb, the oar I used to pull among my comrades.’
“Then I said to him, ‘All this will be done, just as you ask.’
“As we talked, we sat facing each other across the trench, and I kept my sword held out over the blood.

“After him came the soul of my mother, whom I had left alive when I sailed to Troy. I wept bitterly to see her, yet I would not let her come near and drink the blood until I had questioned Teiresias. Then Teiresias came, holding a golden scepter in his hand, and he said, ‘Why have you left the light of day and come to this land of the dead, where there is no joy? Come, step back from the pit and put away your sword, so that I can come close and tell you the truth.’

“So I pushed my sword back into its sheath, and Teiresias drank the blood. When he had drunk, he spoke: ‘You want to hear about your journey home. Know, then, that it will be full of danger and hardship. Poseidon will not easily give up his anger against you, because you took the sight from the eye of his dear son, the Cyclops. Still, you and your comrades may reach home safely, if you can hold yourself and them back when you come to the island of the Three Capes and find the oxen and sheep of the Sun grazing there. If you leave them alone and do them no harm, you may still return to Ithaca, though only after dreadful hardship. If you do not, you will all die. And if you yourself escape, it will be after a long time, having lost all your comrades, and a stranger’s ship will carry you. You will find trouble in your house: violent men who are eating up your wealth while they court your wife.’

“I answered him, ‘So be it, Teiresias. The gods have arranged all this as they wished. But tell me one thing. I see the soul of my dead mother here. She sits near the blood, yet she does not look at me or speak to me. How can she know that I am really her son?’
“Teiresias said, ‘Any of the dead you let drink the blood will speak to you. Any you don’t let drink will leave in silence.’

“So I stayed where I was, and the soul of my mother came near and drank the blood. When she had drunk, she knew her son, and she said, ‘My son, why have you come to the land of darkness while you are still alive? Haven’t you reached home yet?’

“I answered her, ‘I came here to ask Teiresias of Thebes for guidance, and I have not seen my home. Trouble has followed me ever since the day I first went with King Agamemnon to the land of Troy. But tell me, how did you die? Did a wasting illness kill you, or did Artemis[1] strike you down with a sudden arrow? And what of my father and my son? Do they still have what is mine, or have others taken it from them? And my wife, is she faithful to me, or has she married some prince among the Greeks?’

“My mother said, ‘Your wife is faithful, and she sits weeping for you day and night. Your son has your property and takes his proper place at the people’s feasts. But your father no longer comes into the city. He lives in the country. He has no bed to sleep on. In winter he sleeps like the slaves, in the ashes near the fire, and when summer comes, on a pile of leaves in the corner of the vineyard. He grieves deeply as he waits for you to return, and old age weighs heavily on him. As for me, no wasting illness killed me, and Artemis did not strike me with her arrows. I died of longing for you, so painfully did I miss your wisdom and your love.’

“Then I longed to take hold of my mother’s soul. Three times I lunged forward, eager to embrace her, and three times she slipped through my hands like a shadow. I said, ‘What is this, my mother? Are you only a phantom that the queen of the dead has sent me?’ My mother answered, ‘That is how it is with the dead, my son. They no longer have flesh and bones, because the fire consumes those. Their souls are like dreams, flitting here and there. But go back to the light as soon as you can, and tell your wife everything you have seen and heard.’

“After that I left the place and told my comrades to board the ships and cast off the ropes. We climbed aboard and sat down at the benches, and the great stream of Ocean carried us onward, first by our rowing and afterward by the sails we raised.”
[1] Ar’-te-mis

chapters.title: The Sirens; Scylla; the Oxen of the Sun
paragraphs: “It was evening when we came back to Circe’s island. We beached the ship, lay down by the sea, and slept until morning. When day came, we got up and went to Circe’s palace and brought out the body of our comrade Elpenor. We built the funeral pile on the farthest headland, where it juts out into the sea, and burned the dead man with his armor. Then we heaped a mound over his bones, set a pillar on top of the mound, and on top of the pillar we put his oar.

“But Circe knew we had arrived and what we had done. She came and stood among us, with her handmaids bringing plenty of meat, bread, and wine. Then she said, ‘You are reckless, you who have gone down twice into the house of death, which most people see only once. Come now, eat and drink today. Tomorrow you will sail again over the sea. I will tell you the way and explain everything that is going to happen, so that nothing will hold you back on your voyage.’

“So we ate and feasted all that day. When darkness fell over the land, my comrades lay down beside the ship and slept. But Circe took me by the hand, led me away from my company, and asked what I had seen and done. When I had told her my whole story, she said, ‘Now listen to what I will tell you. First you will come to the Sirens, who bewitch every man with their singing. Anyone who comes near them and hears their song never sees his wife or children again. The Sirens enchant him and draw him to the place where they sit, with a great heap of dead men’s bones around them. Row your ship past them. First fill your comrades’ ears with wax, so that none of them hears the song. But if you want to hear it yourself, have them tie you tightly to the mast. Then you can hear the song and come to no harm. And if you beg your comrades to untie you, they must tie the ropes even tighter.

“‘After you have passed the island of the Sirens, you must choose which path to take. On one side are the rocks men call the Wandering Rocks. Not even winged creatures can pass them unharmed. No ship gets by them without damage. All around them the waves toss the timbers of wrecked ships and the bodies of drowned men. Only one ship has ever passed them, the ship Argo, and the waves would have dashed even her against the rocks, but Hera[1] loved Jason[2] and brought her safely through.

“‘Those are on one side. On the other are two more rocks. The first rises to the sky in a sharp peak, and a dark cloud wraps around the peak and never clears away, not in summer and not at harvest. No man could climb this rock, even with twenty hands and feet, for it is steep and smooth. Halfway up the cliff is a cave where Scylla lives, the dreadful monster of the sea. Her voice is no louder than a newborn puppy’s, and her twelve feet are small and stunted. But she has six very long necks, and on each one a head horrible to look at, and in each head three rows of teeth, packed close and full of death. She is hidden up to her middle in the cave, but she sticks her heads out and fishes for dolphins, sea-dogs, or other creatures of the sea, for there are countless herds of them. No ship can pass her unharmed, for with each head she snatches a man off the ship’s deck. Close by, no more than a bowshot away, is the other rock, much lower, with a great fig tree growing on top. Beneath it Charybdis[3] sucks in the water three times a day and spouts it out again three times a day. If you are there when she sucks it in, not even Poseidon could save you. So steer your ship close to Scylla rather than to the other rock, for it is better to lose six men from your ship than your whole company together.’

“When Circe had finished, I said, ‘Tell me, goddess, is there any way I can escape Charybdis on the one side and, on the other, take revenge on this monster when she tries to carry off my comrades as her prey?’

“But the goddess said, ‘You are reckless, and your mind is always on deeds of battle. You would fight the gods themselves! Scylla is not mortal, and there is no defense against her. You will do better to run. If you linger to put on your armor, she will strike again and take as many men as before. So drive your ship on as fast as you can.

“‘After this you will come to the island of the Three Capes, where the herds and flocks of the Sun graze. There are seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep, fifty animals in each. They are never born and never die, and two goddesses tend them. If you do them no harm, you will all return to Ithaca. But if you hurt them, your ship will be wrecked, all your company will die, and you will come home alone, and only after a long delay.’
“With these words the goddess left us. Then I woke my men, and they launched the ship and struck the water with their oars. The goddess sent us a favorable wind, and we raised the sails and rested.

“As we sailed on, I spoke to my companions. ‘Friends,’ I said, ‘it isn’t right that only one or two of us should know what Circe foretold to me. So I will tell you all of it, and then we will know ahead of time what is coming, and whether we are to die or live.’

“First I told them about the Sirens. While I was still speaking, we reached the Sirens’ island. The breeze died away, and the sea lay perfectly still. My comrades lowered the sails and took up the oars. Then I cut a large round of wax in pieces with my sword, softened it in the sun, and pressed it into the ears of my men. After that they tied me hand and foot as I stood upright against the mast. When we had come so close to the shore that a man’s shout could be heard there, the Sirens saw the ship and began to sing. This was their song:

“‘Come here, come closer, famous Odysseus, the great glory of the Greeks. Stop your ship and listen to the voices of the two of us. No one has ever sailed past in a black ship without first hearing the voice that flows from our lips, sweet as honeycomb. Those who hear it enjoy it, and go on their way wiser than before. For we know everything: all that the Greeks and Trojans suffered in the wide land of Troy, and we know all that will happen in the future on the fruitful earth.’

“Then I signaled to my men to untie me, but their ears were plugged. They only bent harder to their oars, and Eurylochus tied me with still more ropes. When we had passed the island, they took the wax out of their ears and set me free.

“Soon afterward they saw smoke and breaking waves, and heard a mighty roar. In their fear the oars slipped from their hands. But I told them to take heart, since my advice had saved them from other dangers in the past. I ordered the rowers to pull as hard as they could. To the helmsman I said, ‘Steer the ship away from the smoke and the surf, and keep close to the cliffs.’ About Scylla I said nothing, afraid that they would lose heart and stop rowing altogether. Then I put on my armor and stood at the bow, waiting for Scylla to appear.

“So we sailed into the strait. My heart was heavy with dread, for Scylla was on one side and Charybdis on the other, sucking down the sea in a terrible way. First she would spew it up again, boiling like a great kettle over a fire, and the spray fell on the very tops of the cliffs on both sides. Then she would gulp the water down again, so that we could see right to her depths, even the white sand on the bottom of the sea. We looked toward her, afraid that we would be destroyed, and while we were looking, Scylla snatched six of my companions out of the ship, the strongest and bravest of them all. When I turned to look at my ship and my crew, I saw their feet and hands, and I heard them calling my name for the last time. A fisherman standing on a headland lowers his long line with bait to catch the fish of the sea, and as he hooks each one, he flings it writhing onto the shore. In just the same way Scylla carried my men writhing up the cliff to her cave. There she ate them, while they screamed to me in terror. Of all the things I have seen on the sea, this was the most pitiful.

“After this we came to the island of the Three Capes, and from my ship I could hear cattle lowing and sheep bleating. Then I remembered what Teiresias had said, when he warned me to avoid the island of the Sun. So I spoke to my comrades. ‘Listen to the advice of Teiresias and Circe,’ I said. ‘They both told me to sail past the island of the Sun, because the worst disaster would strike us there. So row the ship past.’

“That was what I said, but Eurylochus answered angrily. ‘Ulysses, you must never get tired. You must be made of iron, if you forbid us to land on this island, when we are exhausted from hard work and lack of sleep and could rest here so well. And it is reckless of you to order us to sail through the night. Deadly winds spring up at night, and how will we survive if a sudden storm from the west or south strikes our ship and smashes it to pieces? No, let us stay here, eat our meal, and sleep beside the ship, and tomorrow we will sail out over the sea again.’

“So he spoke, and everyone agreed with him. Then I knew that the gods meant to do us harm, and I answered, ‘You are forcing me, since there are many of you and only one of me. But all of you must swear an oath: if you find a herd or a flock here, you will not kill any bull or sheep, but will be content with the food that Circe gave us.’

“They all swore that they would keep this promise. When they had sworn, they moored the ship in a creek where there was a spring of fresh water, and we ate our meal. When we had had enough to eat and drink, we remembered our comrades whom Scylla had snatched from the ship and devoured, and we wept for them until sleep came over us.

“The next morning I spoke to my company. ‘Friends,’ I said, ‘we still have food, both bread and wine. So keep your hands off the flocks and herds, or some disaster will fall on us. They are the flocks and herds of the Sun, a mighty god whose eye nothing can escape.’

“With these words I won them over. But for a whole month the south wind blew without stopping, and no other wind came, except perhaps the east. As long as the bread and wine lasted, the men did not touch the herds, since they were afraid to die. But later, when our supplies were gone, they wandered about the island looking for food, catching fish and birds with hooks, because hunger was pressing them hard. I wandered off by myself, praying to the gods to send us a way out. One day it happened that sleep overcame me, and I lay sleeping far from my companions.

“Meanwhile Eurylochus spoke to the others, with deadly cunning. ‘Friends,’ he said, ‘listen to a man who suffers along with you. Every kind of death is miserable, but the most dreadful of all is death by hunger. So come, let us offer the best of the Sun’s oxen as a sacrifice to the gods in heaven. And we will vow that when we reach Ithaca, we will build the Sun a great temple and decorate it with many rich gifts. But if the god is angry about his oxen and decides to sink our ship, then I would rather drown in the sea than slowly waste away to death on this island.’
“They all agreed to this. Then Eurylochus drove off the fattest of the cattle—they were grazing near the ship—and the men sacrificed it to the gods.

“One of the nymphs who looked after the cattle flew to the Sun with the news of what had been done. Then the Sun spoke among the other gods. ‘Punish the guilty comrades of Ulysses for me now,’ he said. ‘They have killed the herds that I love to look down on, both when I climb up into the sky and when I go down again. If they do not pay the full price for what they have done, I will go down and shine my light among the dead.’
“Then Zeus answered, ‘Keep shining on the earth as before, Sun. My thunderbolt can easily strike the ship of these sinners and smash it in the middle of the sea.’
“I heard all this later from the nymph Calypso, who had heard it from Hermes, the messenger.

“I scolded my comrades angrily, but I could find no cure for what they had done, since the cattle were already dead. For six days my friends feasted on the cattle of the Sun. On the seventh day we launched our ship onto the sea and set sail.

“When we were out of sight of the island of the Three Capes and no other land could be seen, Zeus hung a dark cloud over us. Suddenly the west wind swept down hard on the ship and snapped the ropes that held the mast on both sides. The mast fell backward and cracked the skull of the helmsman, and he dropped into the sea like a diver. At the same moment Zeus hurled his thunderbolt into the ship, and it filled from end to end with the smell of sulphur. My comrades were thrown out of the ship, and I saw them tossed about around it like sea gulls. But I stayed on board until the waves tore the sides away from the keel. Then I bound myself with a leather strap to the mast and the keel, which had been fastened together, and sat on them while the wind drove me along. All night I was driven, and in the morning I came back to Scylla and Charybdis. It was the moment when she was sucking in the waves. A wave lifted me up, and I grabbed hold of the branches of the wild fig tree that grew on the rock. I clung to it for a long time, but could not find a way to climb higher. So I waited until she would spew out the keel and the mast again, for she had swallowed them. When I saw them come up, I let go and dropped from the rock, caught hold of them, and sat on them. I paddled hard with the palms of my hands, and the father of the gods did not allow Scylla to catch sight of me, or I would surely have died. For nine days I drifted, and on the tenth the gods carried me to the island of Calypso.”
[1] He’-ra
[2] Ja’-son
[3] Cha-ryb’-dis

chapters.title: Ithaca
paragraphs: When Ulysses finished his story, there was silence in the hall for a while. Then King Alcinous spoke. “Ulysses, now that you have come to my house, you will not be held back from going home any longer. And as for you, chiefs of the Phaeacians, this is my command. Clothing and gold are already stored for this stranger in a chest. Now let each of us give him a gift as well.”
The princes liked this idea, and each went home. The next day they brought their gifts, and the King himself stowed them under the benches, so that they would not get in the way of the rowers.

When this was done, the princes went to the King’s palace. He sacrificed an ox to Zeus, and they feasted while the minstrel sang. But Ulysses kept looking at the sun, as if he wanted to hurry it down. He was longing to go home, the way a man longs for his supper after driving the plow all day through a field behind a team of oxen, and is very glad when the sun sinks in the west. In the same way Ulysses was glad to see the daylight fade. Then he spoke.

“Pour out the drink offering now, my lord the King, and send me on my way. I say farewell to you all, for you have given me everything my heart desired: noble gifts and an escort to my home. May the gods grant me good luck along with them, and may I find my wife and my friends at home unharmed! And may you stay here happily with your wives and children, with every good thing, and may no evil come near you.”
Then the King said to his squire, “Mix the bowl now and pour out the wine, so that we may pray to Zeus and send the stranger on his way.”
The squire mixed the wine and poured it out, and they all made their offering and prayed.

Then Ulysses stood up and put the cup into the hand of Arete, the Queen. “Farewell, O Queen,” he said, “until old age and death, which no one can escape, come to you! I am going home. May you find joy in your children, in your people, and in your husband the King.”

With these words he stepped over the threshold. Alcinous sent a squire with him to guide him to the ship, and Arete sent maids carrying fresh clothing, bread, and wine. When they reached the ship, the rowers took these things and stowed them in the hold. They also spread a rug and a linen sheet for Ulysses in the back of the ship, so that he could sleep soundly.

When all this was done, Ulysses climbed on board and lay down. The men sat on the benches and untied the cable. As soon as their oars touched the water, a deep sleep fell on him. The ship raced over the waves as fast as four horses pull a chariot across a plain. Not even a hawk, the swiftest of all flying creatures, could have kept up with it.

When the star that announces the morning rose in the sky, the ship neared the island. In Ithaca there is a certain harbor, the harbor of Phorcys[1], the sea god. Two great cliffs on either side of it break the force of the waves, so that a ship that can get into it can lie safely without being tied up. At the head of this harbor stands an olive tree, and close by is a cave sacred to the nymphs. The cave has two gates: one faces north, and men may enter by it, and one faces south, and that one belongs to the gods alone. The Phaeacians steered the ship to this place, because they knew it well. They rowed so hard that she ran half her length up onto the shore. Then they lifted Ulysses out of the stern, still lying in the sheet and the rug that the Queen had given him. He was still asleep. They also took out the gifts that the princes of the Phaeacians had given him and piled them by the trunk of the olive tree, a little way off the road, so that no passer-by would rob him while he slept. After that they went back home.

But Poseidon had not forgotten his anger, and he said to Zeus, “Now I will be held in dishonor among the gods, because mortal men, even these Phaeacians, who are my own kin, pay me no respect. I had decided that this Ulysses would get home only after great suffering. Yet now they have carried him safely across the sea, with more treasure than he would ever have won from Troy, even if he had come back unharmed with his whole share of the spoil.”

Zeus answered him, “What are you saying, lord of the sea? How could the gods dishonor you, the eldest among them? And if men refuse you the worship that is your due, you can punish them however you like. So do as you wish.”

Then Poseidon said, “I would have done it long ago, if I had not feared your anger. But now I will strike this Phaeacian ship as she comes back from taking this man home. That will teach them never to send men home again. And I will cover their city with a great mountain.”
And Zeus answered him, “Do as you wish.”
Poseidon then went down to the land of the Phaeacians and waited until the ship drew near, racing along on her way home. With one blow he turned her to stone and fixed her to the sea floor.
The Phaeacians began asking one another, “Who has stopped our ship on her way home? A moment ago we could see her plainly.”

Then King Alcinous spoke. “The prophecies my father used to tell us have come true. He said that Poseidon was angry with us for carrying men safely across the sea, and that one day the god would strike one of our ships and turn it to stone, and would also cover our city with a great mountain. So now we must stop taking travelers home. Let us offer a sacrifice to Poseidon instead, twelve bulls, so that he will not bury our city under a great mountain.”
So the King said, and the princes did as he ordered.

Meanwhile Ulysses woke up in the land of Ithaca, and he did not recognize it, because Athene had wrapped it in a thick mist. She did this for a good reason, as we will see: she wanted him to be able to carry out his plans safely. Ulysses jumped to his feet and cried out in dismay, “Poor me! What country have I come to now? Are the people here wild and unjust, or do they welcome strangers and fear the gods? Where can I take all this treasure? And where can I go myself? The Phaeacians have surely treated me unfairly. They promised to take me home to my own country, and instead they have left me in a strange land. May Zeus punish them for it! But first let me look over my belongings and count them, in case any of them have been stolen.”
He counted the treasure and found that nothing was missing. Even so, he went on mourning for his homeland.

As he walked along the shore, grieving, Athene came to meet him. She looked like a young shepherd, handsome, with the bearing of a king’s son. Ulysses was glad to see her, though he did not know who she was, and he said, “Friend, you are the first person I have seen in this country. I beg you, protect my belongings and me. But first tell me the truth: what land is this, and who lives here? Is it an island, or part of the mainland?”

The false shepherd answered, “You must be a fool, or else you have come from very far away, if you don’t know this country. Plenty of people know it, in the east and in the west. It is rocky and no good for horses, and it is not very large. But the soil is rich and good for growing grapes, it gets plenty of rain, and it makes fine pasture for cattle and goats. People call it Ithaca. Even in Troy, which they say is very far from this land of Greece, men have heard of Ithaca.”
Ulysses was delighted to hear this. Still, he did not want to say who he was. He preferred to make up a story.

So he said, “Yes, indeed, I heard about Ithaca in Crete. I have only just come from there, with all this wealth, and I left as much again behind for my children. I killed the King’s son, because he wanted to take my share of the plunder. Then some Phoenicians[2] agreed to carry me to Pylos or to Elis,[3] but the wind blew them here instead. While I was asleep they set me down on the shore with my belongings and sailed away.”
This pleased Athene very much. She changed her shape and became a tall, beautiful woman, and she said to Ulysses:—

“It would take a very clever person to trick you. Here you are in your own country, and you still can’t stop telling cunning lies! But let that go. You are the wisest of all mortal men, and I am the best of the gods at giving counsel. I am Athene, daughter of Zeus, and I am always at your side, helping you. Now we will hide your treasure. You must stay quiet and tell no one who you are, and you must put up with many hardships, so that you can win back what is yours.”

Ulysses answered her, “It is hard for any mortal to recognize you, goddess, however wise he may be, because you take so many shapes. When I was fighting at Troy with the other Greeks, you were always kind to me. But after we took Priam’s city and set sail for home, I never saw you again, until you met me in the land of the Phaeacians, comforted me, and led me into their city yourself. Now I beg you, by your father Zeus, tell me the truth. Is this really Ithaca that I see? It seems to me that I have come to some other country, and that you are making fun of me. Tell me, have I truly come to my own land?”

Athene answered, “I will never abandon you, because you are wiser and more prudent than any other man. Anyone else, coming home after so many wanderings, would have rushed to see his wife and children. But you want to test your wife first. Come, I will show you this land of Ithaca, so that you can be sure in your heart. Look! Here is the harbor of Phorcys. Here at the head of the harbor is the olive tree. Here is the pleasant cave that is sacred to the nymphs, and over there is the wooded hill.”

Then the goddess cleared the mist away, and he saw the land. Now he knew it was Ithaca. He knelt down and kissed the ground, and he prayed to the nymphs: “I never thought I would see you again, but now I greet you with love. I will give you many gifts, too, if Athene is willing, in her kindness, to bring me back to my own.” Athene said, “Take heart, and don’t be troubled. First let us put your goods away safely in the secret part of the cave.”
Ulysses carried up the bronze, the gold, and the clothing that the Phaeacians had given him. The two of them stored it all in the cave, and Athene set a great stone across the entrance.

Then Athene said, “Think, man of many schemes, how you will deal with these men, the suitors of your wife, who for three years have sat in your house eating up your wealth. She has put them off with clever answers and many promises, but she is still waiting for you to come home.”
Ulysses replied, “Truly I would have died if not for you. But help me now, as you did long ago at Troy. With you at my side I would fight three hundred men.”

Athene said, “Look, I will make sure that no one recognizes you. I will shrivel the fair skin on your limbs, take the bright hair from your head, and dull your eyes. The suitors will pay no attention to you, and neither your wife nor your son will know you. Go to the swineherd Eumaeus,[4] who lives by the fountain of Arethusa.[5] He is loyal to you and to your house. I will hurry to Sparta, to the house of Menelaus, to bring Telemachus back, since he went there looking for news of you.”

But Ulysses said to the goddess, “Why didn’t you tell him, when you knew everything? Was it so that he too would wander over the seas in great suffering, while others used up his property in the meantime?”

Athene replied, “Don’t worry about him. I guided him myself, so that he would win a good reputation as a son searching for his father. Now he is sitting safely in the hall of Menelaus. Some men are lying in wait to kill him, but they will not get their way. Instead they will die themselves, together with the others who have been eating up your wealth.”

Then she touched him with her rod. His skin withered, the hair on his head fell out, and his skin became like an old man’s. His eyes grew dim. She turned his clothes into filthy, torn rags, black with smoke. Over everything she threw the hide of a big stag, with most of its hair rubbed off. She also gave him a staff, a tattered bag, and a cord to fasten it with.
[1] Phor’-cys
[2] Phoe-ni’-ci-ans
[3] E’-lis
[4] Eu-mae’- us.
[5] A-re- thu’-sa.

chapters.title: Eumaeus, the Swineherd
paragraphs: Athene left for Lacedaemon to bring Telemachus home, and Ulysses went to the house of Eumaeus, the swineherd. There was a large courtyard, with twelve sties for the sows and four watchdogs as fierce as wild beasts. Fifty pigs were penned in each sty, but there were fewer hogs, because the suitors kept eating them at their feasts. There were only three hundred and sixty in all. The swineherd himself was making sandals. Three of his men were out in the fields with the pigs, and a fourth was driving a fat beast to the city, to be meat for the suitors. When Ulysses came near, the dogs rushed at him. He dropped his staff and sat down, and even so he might have been hurt on his own doorstep, but the swineherd ran out and chased the dogs away with stones. He spoke to his master, though he did not know him, and said:—

“Old man, the dogs almost killed you. That would have been a shame and a sorrow to me, and I have plenty of other sorrows already. Here I sit grieving for my master and raising fat pigs for other people to eat, while he may be wandering hungry over the sea or in some foreign land, if he is still alive. But come to my house, old man, and tell me who you are and what troubles you have suffered.”
Then the swineherd led him to his hut and sat him down on a seat of brushwood, with the hide of a wild goat spread over it. The hide was large and soft, and Eumaeus usually slept on it himself.
Ulysses was very glad of this welcome, and he said, “May Zeus and the other gods give you your heart’s desire, for being so kind to me!”

The swineherd answered, “It would be wicked of me to turn a stranger away, because strangers and beggars come from Zeus. But for slaves like us, who live in fear of our master, even a small gift matters. The gods have kept my master from coming home. If he had returned, he would surely have given me a house, a piece of land, and a good wife as well, since that is what masters give to servants who serve them well. My master would have rewarded me richly if he had stayed at home. But now he is dead. He went to Troy too, so that Agamemnon and his brother Menalaus could take revenge on the Trojans.”

Then he went to the sties, brought back two young pigs, singed them, cut them into pieces, and roasted them on spits. When they were cooked, he set them in front of the beggar. He also mixed wine in a bowl of ivy-wood, sat down across from his guest, and told him to eat. “Eat what food I can give you. The fat hogs are for the suitors to devour. These men have no pity and no fear of the gods. They must have heard that my master is dead, they behave so wickedly. They don’t court the way other suitors do, and they don’t go back to their own houses. They just sit at their ease and eat up our wealth without limit. Once my master had more possessions than anyone could count. No one in Ithaca or on the mainland had so much. Listen to the total: on the mainland he had twenty herds of cattle, and as many flocks of sheep, droves of pigs, and herds of goats. Here at the far end of this island he also had eleven flocks of goats. Every day they take one of the goats for the suitors, and I take them the best of the hogs.”

So he spoke, and Ulysses ate the meat and drank the wine. He said not a word, because he was planning the suitors’ deaths. At last he spoke. “My friend, who was this master of yours that you talk about? You say he died trying to take revenge for King Menelaus. Tell me, because I may have seen him. I have traveled far.”

Eumaeus said, “No, old man, all travelers talk like that, and we never hear any truth from them. Every vagabond who comes to this island has to be seen by our Queen, and she asks him many questions, weeping all the while. I’m sure you would tell a wonderful tale too. But I know that Ulysses is dead, and the birds of the air or the fish of the sea have eaten him.”

But the false beggar said, “Listen, I swear to you that Ulysses will return. As soon as it happens, you must give me the reward for good news. You will give me a cloak and a tunic. Until then I will take nothing, however badly I need it. Let Zeus be my witness, and this welcoming hearth of Ulysses where I have come, that everything will happen just as I say. Ulysses will return this year. Yes, as the moon wanes he will come, and take revenge on everyone who dishonors his name.”

Eumaeus replied, “It will never be me, old man, who pays that reward for good news. Ulysses will never come home again. But let us talk about something else. Don’t remind me of these things any more. My heart is full of sorrow whenever anyone mentions my master. As for your oath, let it be. I pray with all my heart that Ulysses will return. That is what I want, and what his wife wants, and old Laertes, and Telemachus. And now I am worried about Telemachus too. I thought he would turn out no worse a man than his father. But someone, whether a god or a man I can’t say, took away his good sense, and he went to Pylos to look for news of his father. Now the suitors are lying in wait for him, because they want the whole line of Ulysses to die out in this land. Come, old man, tell me who you are and where you come from. What ship did you come on? I’m sure you came to Ithaca by ship.”

Then Ulysses answered, “If we had food and wine to last us a whole year, and could sit here quietly and talk while others went off to work, I would still take that long to tell you all the troubles I have suffered on this earth.”

Then he told a false tale. He said he was a Cretan who had been shipwrecked, and that after many hardships he had reached Thesprotia,[1] where he had heard about Ulysses. When he sailed from there, the sailors planned to sell him as a slave, but he broke his bonds and swam ashore when they were near the island, and hid in the woods.

Then the swineherd said, “Stranger, your story of all you have suffered has touched my heart. But I fear you are wrong to say that Ulysses will return. I know well that the gods hated him, because they did not strike him down while he was fighting the Trojans, or afterward among his friends, once the war was over. If they had, the whole army would have built him a great burial mound, and he would have won lasting fame for himself and for his children. Instead he has died without glory in the storms of the sea. As for me, I live off by myself with the pigs, and I never go into the city, except when some news of my master has arrived, no one knows from where. Then all the people sit around the messenger and question him, both those who long for their lord’s return and those who enjoy eating up his wealth without paying for it. But I no longer care to ask questions, not since a certain Aetolian[2] fooled me with his story. He too had killed a man and had wandered through many lands, and when he came to my house, I treated him kindly. This fellow claimed he had seen my master with the King of Crete, mending his ships that a storm had broken. He also said that Ulysses would come home in summer, or at harvest time, and would bring great riches with him. But you, old man, do not try to win my favor with lies, or to comfort me with empty words.”

But Ulysses answered, “Truly, you are slow to believe. Even an oath has not persuaded you. Come, let us make a bargain, and let the gods be our witnesses. If your master returns, you will give me a cloak and a tunic and send me on my way, wherever I want to go. But if he does not come back as I have said, then have your men throw me off a high cliff, so that others will be afraid to deceive.”

Then the swineherd said, “I would win a fine reputation among men, wouldn’t I, if I welcomed you into my house and then turned around and killed you! I could hardly pray to Zeus with a clear conscience after that. But it is time for supper, and I wish my men would come back so that we could prepare a meal.”

As he was speaking, the pigs and the other swineherds came up. Eumaeus called to his companions, “Bring the best of the pigs, because I want to feed a guest who has come from far away. We put up with a great deal of work for these animals, while others eat them up and give nothing back.”

So they brought a hog five years old. The swineherd lit a fire, and first he threw some bristles from the hog into the flames, as an honor to the gods. Then he killed the animal and prepared the meat. He cut it into seven portions. One he set aside for the nymphs and Hermes, and he gave one of the rest to each man. But Ulysses received the best portion, the chine.
Ulysses was pleased. “Eumaeus,” he said, “may Zeus hold you dear, because you have treated me so kindly.”
Eumaeus answered, “Eat, stranger, and enjoy what you have. The gods give us some things and keep back others.”

The night was cold, and it rained without stopping, because the west wind, which always brings rain, was blowing. Ulysses wanted to test the swineherd, to see whether he would give up his own cloak or tell someone else to do it. So when they were about to go to sleep, he said:
“Listen to me. I wish I were young again, with my strength unbroken, as in the days when we fought before the city of Troy.

“Once we set an ambush near the walls of Troy. Menelaus, Ulysses and I were its leaders. We lay hidden in the reeds, the night was cold, and snow covered our shields. The others all had cloaks, but I had left mine behind at the ships. So when the night was three parts gone, I said to Ulysses, ‘Here I am without a cloak. I think I will freeze to death before long.’ He quickly thought of a remedy, since he was always ready with a plan. He said to me, ‘Hush, in case someone hears you.’ Then he said to the others, ‘I have had a warning in a dream. We are very far from the ships, and in danger. Someone should run to the ships, to King Agamemnon, and ask him to send more men to help us.’ One man jumped up and ran, throwing off his cloak as he went. I took it and slept warmly in it. If I were tonight what I was then, I would not lack such kindness even now.”

Then Eumaeus said, “That is well told, old man. You shall have a cloak to cover you. But in the morning you must put on your own rags again. Perhaps, though, when the son of Ulysses comes, he will give you new clothes.”

With that he got up and made a bed for Ulysses near the fire, out of sheepskins and goatskins. When Ulysses lay down, Eumaeus threw over him a thick cloak that he kept for the times when a great storm came up. Then he went out to sleep beside the boars and guard them. Ulysses was glad to see how carefully he looked after his master’s property, even though his master had been gone so long.
[1] Thes-pro’ti-a.
[2] AE-to’-li-an.

chapters.title: The Return of Telemachus
paragraphs: All this time Telemachus was staying in Sparta with King Menelaus, and Nestor’s son was with him. Athene went to him there. She found Nestor’s son sunk in sleep, but Telemachus could not sleep for thinking of his father. Athene stood beside him and said:

“Telemachus, it is not right for you to stay away from home any longer, since there are people there who are plundering and eating up your property. Go and wake your host Menelaus, and ask him to send you on your way. Your mother’s father and her brothers are urging her to marry Eurymachus,[1] because he has outdone all the other suitors in his gifts. Listen also to something else. The boldest of the suitors are lying in wait for you in the strait between Ithaca and Samos, eager to kill you before you can reach home again. So keep your ship far away from that place, and sail by night as well as by day, and one of the gods will send you a fair wind. And when you arrive in the land of Ithaca, send your ship and your crew on to the city, but go yourself to the swineherd Eumaeus, who has always been loyal to you. Spend the night there, and tell him to go to the city the next day and bring your mother word that you are safely back.”
Then Telemachus woke Nestor’s son by nudging him with his heel, and said, “Wake up, son of Nestor. Bring out your horses and harness them to the chariot, so we can be on our way.”

But Peisistratus answered, “We can’t drive through the dark, however eager we are to leave. It will be dawn soon. Wait until Menelaus brings his gifts and puts them in the chariot, and sends you on your way. A guest should think of the host who shows him such kindness.”
When morning came and Menelaus had gotten out of bed, Telemachus said to him, “Menelaus, please send me home to my own country as quickly as you can, because I am very anxious to get there.”

Menelaus answered him, “I won’t keep you long, since you want to go back. But wait until I bring my gifts and put them in the chariot. Let me also tell the women to prepare a meal in my hall, because it honors me, and it does you good, to eat well before you set out on a long journey. But if you would like to travel farther through the land, then let me go with you. We will visit many cities, and none will send us away empty-handed.”

But Telemachus said, “No, Menelaus. I would rather go straight back to my own land, because I left no one to watch over my property. It would be terrible if I died while searching for my father, or lost some valuable thing from my house.”

Then Menelaus told his wife and the maids to prepare the meal, and he told his squire to light a fire and roast some meat. He himself went to his treasury, with Helen and his son. From it he took a double cup, and he told his son to carry a silver mixing bowl. Helen took from her chests a robe that she had made with her own hands. It was the most beautiful of all, and it shone like a star, and it lay beneath all the others.

Then Menelaus said, “Take this mixing bowl. It is made of silver, but its rim is finished with gold. The god Hephaestus[2] made it with his own hands, and the King of the Sidonians[3] gave it to me. I give you this cup as well.”

Then lovely Helen came, holding the robe in her hands, and said, “Take this, dear child, as a keepsake of Helen’s handiwork. Keep it for your wedding day, for your bride to wear. Until then, let your mother take care of it. And now may you return happily to your native country and your home!”
Then they sat down to eat and drink. When they had finished, Telemachus and Nestor’s son harnessed the horses and climbed into the chariot.
Menelaus came out carrying wine in a golden cup, so that they could pour an offering to the gods before they left. He stood in front of the horses and said:
“Farewell, brave young men, and give my greetings to Nestor. He was like a father to me when we were fighting the war against Troy.”
Telemachus answered him, “We will do that. And may the gods grant that I find my father at home, and can tell him how kindly you received me!”

But just as he spoke, an eagle flew up on his right, carrying a goose in its claws that it had snatched from the farmyard. Men and women ran after it, shouting loudly. It flew across in front of the horses, still keeping to the right, and when they saw it, they were glad.
Then Nestor’s son said, “Think about it, Menelaus! Did Zeus send this sign for us, or for you?”

While Menelaus was still pondering the matter, Helen spoke up. “Hear me, while I tell you what the gods have put into my heart. Just as this eagle came down from the hill where it was raised and snatched the goose from the house, so Ulysses will come back to his home after his long wanderings and take his revenge. Indeed, even now he is there, plotting evil for the suitors.”

Then they left and raced across the plain. When they reached Pylos the next day, Telemachus said to Peisistratus, “Son of Nestor, will you be a friend to me and do what I ask? Leave me at my ship. Don’t take me past it, or your father, the old man, will keep me against my will out of kindness, when I am truly eager to get home.”

Nestor’s son agreed. He turned his horses toward the shore and the ship. When they got there, he took out the gifts and put them in the stern of the ship. Then he called Telemachus and said, “Climb into your ship now and sail, before I can get home. I know well that my father will come down and ask you to return with him to his house. And if he finds you here, he certainly won’t go back without you, he is so stubborn.”
Telemachus told his companions to climb aboard the ship, and they did.
They put out to sea, and Athene sent a following wind that carried them swiftly along.

Meanwhile Ulysses was sitting with the swineherd and his men, eating supper. Ulysses wanted to test the man’s temper, and he said, “In the morning I would like to go to the city, to the house of Ulysses, so that I won’t be a burden to you. Perhaps the suitors would give me a meal. I could serve them well. No man can light a fire, or split wood, or carve meat, or pour wine better than I can.”

“No,” said the swineherd, “you had better not go among the suitors, they are so proud and lawless. Their servants are not at all like you. They are young and handsome and elegantly dressed, and their hair is shining with oil. Stay here. You are no burden to us. And when the son of Ulysses comes, he will give you, perhaps, a cloak and a tunic.”

Ulysses answered, “May Zeus bless you for your kindness, because you have put an end to my wandering. Surely nothing is harder on a man than wandering, though hunger forces him to it. Now tell me about the mother of Ulysses, and about his father. Are they still alive?”
