Then the swineherd said, “I will tell you everything. Laertes, the father of Ulysses, is still alive, but every day he prays to die. He grieves for his son, who is far away from home, and for his wife, who is dead. It was her death that made him old before his time. And she died of grief for her son. I received much kindness from her while she lived, but now I have lost it. As for my lady Penelope, a great trouble has fallen on her house: a plague of evil-minded men.”
[1] Eu-rym’-a-chus.
[2] He-phaes’-tus.
[3] Si-do’-ni-ans.

chapters.title: Ulysses and Telemachus
paragraphs: Telemachus sailed safely to the island of Ithaca and landed at the spot nearest the swineherd’s house. There they ran the ship ashore and secured it with anchors at the bow and ropes at the stern. Then they went ashore and prepared a meal.
When they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus said, “Take the ship on to the city now. I will come there in the evening, after I have seen my farm, and then I will pay you your wages.”
Meanwhile the herdsman and Ulysses had lit a fire and were getting breakfast ready.
Ulysses heard a man’s footsteps, and since the dogs were not barking, he said to Eumaeus, “Look! Some comrade or friend is coming, because the dogs are not barking.”

Even as he spoke, Telemachus appeared in the doorway. The swineherd dropped the bowl in which he was mixing wine, ran to him, and kissed his head, his eyes and his hands. As a father kisses his only son when he comes back to him from a far country after ten years, so the swineherd kissed Telemachus. When Telemachus came in, the false beggar, who was in fact his father, stood up and would have given him his seat, but Telemachus would not let him. When they had eaten and drunk, Telemachus asked the swineherd who the stranger was.
The swineherd told him what he had heard, and then added, “I put him in your hands. Do as you wish.”

But Telemachus answered, “No, Eumaeus. Am I master in my own house? Don’t the suitors eat it up? And doesn’t my mother wonder whether to stay with me, remembering the great Ulysses who was her husband, or to follow one of the men who court her? I will certainly give this stranger food and clothing and a sword, and I will send him wherever he wants to go. But I don’t want him going among the suitors, they are so arrogant and violent.”

Then Ulysses said, “But why do you put up with these men? Do the people hate you, so that you can’t take revenge on them? Don’t you have relatives to help you? As for me, I would rather die than see such shameful things done in a house of mine.”

Telemachus answered, “My own people don’t hate me. But I have no relatives to turn to. My grandfather had only one son, Laertes, and Laertes had only one son, Ulysses, and Ulysses had no child but me. That is why these men are eating up my property, and they may well take my life too. Still, the gods will decide those things. But you, Eumaeus, go to Penelope and tell her I’ve come back. Don’t let anyone else find out, because they are plotting against me. I’ll stay here in the meantime.”

So Eumaeus left. After he had gone, Athene appeared, in the shape of a tall, beautiful woman. Telemachus did not see her, since the immortal gods do not show themselves to everyone. But Ulysses saw her, and so did the dogs, which whimpered with fear. She made a sign to Ulysses, and he went outside. Then she said:—
“Don’t keep the truth from your son. Plan with him how you will kill the suitors, and know that I am with you.”

Then she touched him with her golden wand. First she gave him a fresh linen robe and a new tunic. She also made him taller and more handsome to look at. His skin grew darker, his cheeks filled out again, and the beard spread black across his chin.
When she had done this, she went away. Ulysses walked back into the hut, and his son stared at him in amazement. He was afraid that this might be a god.

“Stranger,” he said, “you are certainly not the man you were a moment ago. You are wearing different clothes, and the color of your skin has changed. You must be some god from heaven. Stay a little while, so we can offer you a sacrifice, and please have mercy on us!”
Ulysses replied, “I am no god. I am your father, the one you have searched for with so much heartache.”
As he said this, he kissed his son, and a tear rolled down his face, though until then he had always held his tears back.

But Telemachus still doubted that this could really be his father. He answered, “You can’t be my father. Some god is tricking me to pile sorrow on sorrow. No mortal man could do this, making himself young one moment and old the next, whenever he likes. A moment ago you were old and dressed in wretched rags, and now you look like one of the gods in heaven.”

But Ulysses said to him, “Telemachus, you shouldn’t be so amazed that your father has come home. It really is I, and I have come at last, in the twentieth year, after suffering much and wandering through many lands. What you are wondering at is Athene’s doing. She is the one who makes me look like an old beggar one time and a young man in fine clothes the next.”

With these words he sat down again. Telemachus threw his arms around his father’s neck and wept, and his father wept too. When they had dried their tears, Telemachus said, “Tell me how you got back, father.”

So Ulysses told him: “The Phaeacians brought me home from their country while I slept. They sent me off with many gifts, and I have hidden them in a cave. I came here on Athene’s advice, so that we could plan together how to kill the suitors. Now tell me how many suitors there are and what sort of men they are. Can the two of us fight them, or must we get help from others?”

Telemachus said, “I know you are a great and wise warrior, father, but we cannot do this. There aren’t ten of these men, or even twenty. There are fifty-two from Dulichium[1], twenty-four from Samos, twenty from Zacynthus[2], and twelve from Ithaca. They also have Medon the herald, a minstrel, and servants.”

Ulysses said, “In the morning, go home and mix with the suitors, and I will come later disguised as an old beggar. If they treat me shamefully, put up with it, even if they drag me to the door. Just say a few sensible words to them if you like, though they won’t listen, because their doom is near. Remember this too: when I give you a sign, take all the weapons out of the hall and hide them in your room. If they ask why you are doing it, tell them you are getting the weapons out of the smoke, since they are no longer the weapons Ulysses left behind when he went to Troy, but have been dirtied by the smoke. Say also that you are afraid the men might start a quarrel over their cups, and that it is not wise to have weapons within reach, because the sight of steel tempts a man to fight. But keep back two swords, two spears and two shields. They will be for you and me. And let no one know I have come back, not Laertes, not the swineherd, and not even Penelope herself.”

Meanwhile the ship of Telemachus reached the city. A herald went to the palace with the news for Penelope, so she would not worry about her son. The herald and the swineherd arrived together, since they had the same errand. The herald announced to the maids, “My Queen, your son is back from Pylos!” But the swineherd went to Penelope alone and told her everything Telemachus had ordered him to say. When he had finished, he turned around and went home to his house and his pigs.

The suitors were uneasy, and Eurymachus said, “Telemachus has done a bold thing. He has finished the journey we said he would never finish. So let us gather some rowers and send a ship to tell our friends to come back as fast as they can.”

But even as he was speaking, Amphinomus[3] turned around and saw the ship in the harbor, with the men lowering its sails. He laughed and said, “There is no need to send a message. The men are here already. Perhaps some god told them, or perhaps they saw the ship of Telemachus sail past and couldn’t catch it.”

Then all the suitors went together to the meeting place, and Antinous stood up and said, “Look how the gods have rescued this man! All day long our scouts took turns watching from the headlands, and at sunset we didn’t rest on the shore but sailed on the sea, waiting for morning. Still, some god has brought him home. All the same, we will bring him to a bad end, because as long as he lives we will never get what we want. We must hurry, before he calls the people together and tells them how we plotted against him. Then they will hate us, and we will be driven out of the land. So let us kill him, either in the fields or on the road. Then we will divide his possessions among us, and give his house to his mother and to whoever marries her.”

Then Amphinomus spoke—none of the suitors had a more thoughtful heart than he—“Friends, I don’t want Telemachus to be killed. It is a terrible thing to kill the son of a king. First let us ask the gods for guidance. If the oracles of Zeus approve, I will kill him myself. But if they forbid it, I ask you to hold back.”
With that, they left the meeting place and went to the house of Ulysses.

Meanwhile Penelope had heard from Medon the herald that the suitors were plotting to kill her son. So she went to the hall with her maids, stood in the doorway holding her veil in front of her face, and said:—

“Antinous, people say you give the best advice and speak better than any of the princes of Ithaca. But in truth, that is how I find you. Are you plotting to kill my son, with no respect for the gods and no memory of kindnesses done to you? Don’t you remember how your father fled to this house, afraid of the people’s anger? Yet now you are wasting the property of the very man who sheltered him, and you want to kill his son.”

But Eurymachus answered, “Take heart, wise Penelope, and don’t let this trouble you. The man has not been born, and never will be, who raises a hand against Telemachus while I am alive on this earth. Many times Ulysses sat me on his knee, gave me roasted meat, and held the wine cup to my lips. So Telemachus is the dearest of men to me. Don’t be afraid that the suitors will kill him.”
He said this as if to comfort her, but all the while he was plotting her son’s death.
After this she went to her room and wept for her husband until Athene let sweet sleep fall on her eyes.
Meanwhile the swineherd was returning to his hut. But before he arrived, Athene changed Ulysses back into the likeness of a beggar, so that Eumaeus would not recognize him and tell Penelope.
Telemachus asked him, “Is there any word from town? Are the suitors back from lying in wait for me, or are they still watching for my ship?”

Eumaeus answered, “I didn’t think of going around the city asking questions, but I will tell you what I know. The messenger from your crew joined me on the way and was the first to give the Queen the news. This much I also know: I saw a ship coming into the harbor with many men aboard, and spears and shields. Maybe those were the suitors, but I can’t say for certain.”
Then Telemachus looked at his father, but he avoided the swineherd’s eye.
[1] Du-lich’-i-um.
[2] Za-cyn’-thus.
[3] Am-phi’-no-mus.

chapters.title: Ulysses in his Home
paragraphs: When morning came, Telemachus said to the swineherd, “I’m going to the city, because my mother won’t be content until she sees my face. You take this stranger to the city, so he can beg for his bread from anyone willing to give it.”

Ulysses spoke up. “I don’t like being left here either, my friend. It is better for a man to beg for bread in town than in the fields. You go ahead, and I’ll follow as soon as the sun is warm, because my clothes are very poor and I’m afraid the cold will get the better of me.”

So Telemachus went on his way, plotting evil against the suitors the whole time. When he reached the house, his nurse Eurycleia saw him first and kissed him. Penelope also came down from her room, threw her arms around him, and kissed him on the face and on both eyes. She said, “You’ve come back, Telemachus, light of my eyes! I never thought I would see you again. But tell me, what news did you get of your father?”
Telemachus then repeated everything Nestor and Menelaus had said to him.

Meanwhile the suitors were amusing themselves, throwing weights and aiming spears on a level piece of ground. When it was time for supper, Medon the herald said, “Come, let’s eat. Meat in season is a good thing.”
So they prepared a feast.

Meanwhile Eumaeus and the false beggar were on their way to the city. As they drew near, Melanthius[1] the goatherd met them and spoke abusively to Eumaeus, scolding him for bringing this beggar to the city. He came up close and kicked Ulysses on the thigh, but he did not knock him off the path. Ulysses thought for a moment whether to strike him with his club and kill him, or to throw him to the ground. But he decided it was better to endure it.

So they went on to the palace. At the door of the courtyard lay the dog Argus, whom Ulysses had raised with his own hands in the old days. But Ulysses had sailed to Troy before the dog was fully grown. In his prime, men had used him for hunting wild goats, roe deer and hares. Now he lay on a dunghill, swarming with vermin. He knew his master at once, and though he could not get close to him, he wagged his tail and drooped his ears.
When Ulysses saw him, he wiped away a tear and said, “This is strange, Eumaeus, that such a dog of so fine a breed should lie here on a dunghill.”

Eumaeus answered, “He belongs to a master who died far away. When Ulysses had him long ago, he was the strongest and swiftest of dogs. But now my dear lord has died far from home, and the careless women don’t look after him. When the master is away, the slaves neglect their duty. A man who is made a slave loses half his virtue as a man.”

As he spoke, the dog Argus died. He had waited twenty years, and at last he had seen his master. After this the two men entered the hall. When Telemachus saw them, he took bread and meat from the basket, as much as his hands could hold, and told a servant to carry it to the beggar and to say that he could go around among the suitors asking for gifts. So Ulysses went, holding out his hand as if he were used to begging. Some gave to him out of pity, and some asked who he was. But Antinous was the most shameless of all. Ulysses came to him and told him how he had once had great wealth and power, how he had gone to Egypt, and how he had been sold as a slave in Cyprus. Antinous mocked him, saying:—
“Get away from my table, or you’ll find a worse Egypt and a harsher Cyprus than the ones you’ve known.”
Then Ulysses said, “Your soul is evil, though your body is handsome. You sit at another man’s feast, yet you won’t give me anything.”

Then Antinous grabbed the footstool from under his feet and hit Ulysses with it. But Ulysses stood firm as a rock, and in his heart he thought of revenge. He went and sat down at the door. Sitting there, he said:—
“Hear me, suitors of the Queen! Antinous has struck me because I am poor. May the curse of the hungry fall on him before his wedding day!”
Antinous said, “Sit still, stranger, and eat your bread in silence, or the young men will drag you out of the house and strip the flesh from your bones.”

He said this in his arrogance, but the others blamed him. “Antinous, you did wrong to strike the wanderer. There is a doom on such deeds, if there is any god in heaven. The gods often take the shape of men and go through cities, to see whether people deal justly or unjustly.”
But Antinous paid no attention. Telemachus felt a great sorrow in his heart at seeing his father struck. Yet he shed no tear. He sat in silence, planning evil against the suitors.
When Penelope heard that the stranger had been struck in the hall, she said to her maids, “May Apollo the archer strike Antinous in return!”
Then Eurynome[2], who kept the house, answered, “If only our prayers could be granted! Not one of these wicked men would live to see another day.”
Penelope replied, “Yes, nurse, they are all our enemies, but Antinous is the worst. He is as hateful as death.”

Then Penelope called the swineherd and said, “Go and bring this stranger to me. I want to greet him and ask whether he has heard any news of Ulysses, or perhaps even seen him with his own eyes, since he seems to have wandered far.”

Eumaeus answered, “This man will win your heart, my Queen! I kept him in my hut for three days, and in all that time he never stopped telling me about his troubles. Just as a singer of beautiful songs holds people spellbound, so he held me. He says he is a Cretan, that he has heard news of Ulysses, that Ulysses is still alive, and that he is bringing a great deal of wealth home with him.”
Then Penelope said, “Go and call the man, so that I can speak with him. If only Ulysses would really come back! He and his son would soon make these men pay for all the wrongs they have done!”

Just as she said this, Telemachus sneezed, and the whole house echoed with the sound. Penelope spoke to Eumaeus again. “Call this stranger now. Did you not notice the good omen, how my son sneezed just as I spoke? I tell you, this vengeance will come, and not one of them will escape it. And as for this stranger, if I find that he has told the truth, I will give him a new cloak and tunic.”

So the swineherd said to the stranger, “Penelope wants to speak with you and ask about her husband. If she finds that you have told the truth, she will give you a cloak and a tunic, and you will be free to beg anywhere in the land.”

But the false beggar answered, “I would gladly tell Penelope the story of her husband, for I know him well. But I am afraid of these suitors. Just now, when this man hit me for no reason, nobody stopped the blow, not even Telemachus. So go, and ask the Queen to wait until the sun has set.”
So the swineherd went back, and as he stepped over the threshold Penelope said, “You have not brought him! What is the wanderer thinking? A beggar who is shy knows his trade poorly.”
But the swineherd replied, “He is wise, my lady, to fear the violence of these insolent men. He wants you to wait until sunset, and in fact it is better for you to speak with him alone.”
Then Penelope said, “Very well. The stranger is a sensible man. These men are certainly more insolent than any others.”

Then the swineherd went into the crowd of suitors and spoke to Telemachus, bringing his head close so that nobody else would hear. “I am going to look after things at the farm. Watch carefully what happens here. Many of the people hold a grudge against us. May Zeus destroy them!”
Telemachus answered, “Go, as you say, and come back in the morning, bringing animals for sacrifice.”
So the swineherd left, and the suitors went on feasting and enjoying themselves in the hall.
[1] Me-lan’-thi-us.
[2] Eu-ryn’-o-me.

chapters.title: Ulysses in his Home (continued)
paragraphs: After a while a beggar arrived from the city. He was huge, and could eat and drink enormous amounts, but his strength did not match his size. The young men called him Irus[1], because he ran their errands, just as Iris[2] was the messenger of Zeus. He said to Ulysses:—
“Get out of the way, old man, or I will drag you out. The young men want it that way right now, but I would be ashamed to hit someone like you.”
Ulysses answered, “There is room here for both of us. Take whatever you can get; I do not envy you anything. But take care not to anger me, or I will hurt you, old as I am.”
But Irus would not listen to words of peace. He kept on daring Ulysses to fight.
When Antinous saw this, he was delighted. He said, “This is the best entertainment I have seen in this house. These two beggars want to fight. Let us hurry and set them against each other.”

The others liked the idea, and Antinous spoke again. “Listen, suitors of the Queen! We have set aside these goat paunches for our supper. Let us agree that whichever of these two wins may choose the one he likes best, and from now on he will eat with us, and no other beggar will be allowed to sit in his place.”
Then Ulysses said, “It is hard for an old man to fight a young one. Still, I will do it. But all of you must swear to me that no one will strike me a foul blow while I fight this man.”

Telemachus said that it would be so, and all of them agreed. After this Ulysses tied his clothes up for the fight. Everyone there saw how great and strong his thighs were, how broad his shoulders, and how mighty his arms. They said to one another, “There will be very little left of Irus, the way this beggar is built.” As for Irus himself, he would have crept away out of sight, but the men who were assigned to dress him for the fight forced him to come forward.
Then Antinous said, “What is this, you braggart? You are afraid of this old man, who is so wretched as it is?”

So the two men came together. Ulysses wondered whether he should strike the fellow dead or just knock him to the ground. The second seemed the better choice. So when Irus threw his punch, Ulysses hit him on the jaw and broke the bone. Irus fell to the ground howling, and blood poured from his mouth.

Then all the suitors burst out laughing. But Ulysses dragged the man out of the hall and propped him against the wall of the courtyard. He put a staff in his hand and said, “Sit there and keep the dogs and pigs away from the door. And do not dare to play the lord over other men again, not even over strangers and beggars, or something worse will happen to you.”

Then Antinous gave Ulysses a large paunch, and Amphinomus gave him two loaves of bread and drank his health from a cup, saying, “Good luck to you in the days ahead, though you seem to have bad fortune now!”
[1] I’-rus
[2] I’-ris

chapters.title: Ulysses Is Discovered by his Nurse
paragraphs: When the suitors had gone, Ulysses said to Telemachus, “Come, let us hide the weapons that are in the hall. If any of the suitors ask about them, you will say, ‘I have moved them away from the smoke, because they are not what they were when Ulysses left. The breath of the fire has tarnished them. And I had another reason too: I did not want you to quarrel and wound one another when you are flushed with wine, for the sight of iron tempts a man to strike.’ That is what you will tell the suitors.”
Then Telemachus said to Eurycleia, the nurse, “Lock the women in their rooms until I have put my father’s weapons away in the armory. The smoke in the hall has dulled them.”
The nurse answered, “I wish, my child, that you would always take such care of your father’s belongings! But tell me, who will carry the light, if you will not let any of the women go ahead of you?”
Telemachus said, “This stranger will do it, for I will not have anyone eat my bread without working for it.”

So the nurse locked the women in their rooms, and Ulysses and his son began carrying the shields, helmets and spears from the hall into the armory. Athene walked in front of them the whole way, holding a golden lamp that gave off a lovely light. Telemachus said, “Father, this is truly a marvel that I am seeing! Look, the walls, the beams and the pillars are glowing as if they were on fire. A god must be doing this.”
But Ulysses answered, “Be quiet. Keep this to yourself and do not ask about it. Now go to bed and sleep, for I want to talk with your mother.”
Telemachus withdrew to his bedroom and fell asleep. Ulysses stayed behind by himself in the hall, working out in his mind how to put the suitors to death.

Then Penelope came downstairs and sat by the fire, in a chair skillfully made of silver and ivory, with a footstool that was part of the chair. Soon the maidens came in. They took away the scraps of food that were left and the cups the suitors had drunk from, and piled fresh logs on the fire.
Then Penelope called to the nurse. “Nurse, bring a bench with a fleece on it, so that the stranger can sit and tell me his story.”
So the nurse brought the bench and the fleece, and Ulysses sat down. Penelope said, “Stranger, let me ask you first: who are you? Where do you come from? What is your city, and who was your father?”

Ulysses answered, “Ask me anything else you like, but do not ask me my name, my family or my homeland, for I would weep as I thought of them. I am a man of many sorrows, and it is not right to grieve and weep in someone else’s house.”

Penelope replied, “Stranger, I am weighed down with troubles. The princes of the islands around us, and of Ithaca itself, are courting me against my will and eating up my house. I have tried in vain to escape their courtship. Athene put an idea into my heart, and I told them, ‘Noble young men who want to marry me, now that Ulysses is dead, be patient, though you are eager to hurry the marriage, until I have finished this burial cloth for Laertes. It would be shameful if a man who had owned so much wealth should lie in his grave without one.’ So I spoke, and they agreed. For three years I fooled them, weaving the cloth by day and unraveling it by night, but in the fourth year my maids betrayed me. Now I have no way out of marriage. My parents urge me to it, and my son is angry that these men are eating up his property, for he is now old enough to run his own house. But come, tell me what family you come from, for you were not born from an oak tree or a rock, as the old stories say.”

Ulysses said, “If you still want to know about my family, I will tell you. But you will bring me more sorrow than I must already bear, for it is painful for a man who has wandered far and suffered much to speak of it.”

So Ulysses told his story. It was false, but it seemed true. Penelope wept as she listened. As snow melts on the hills when the southeast wind blows and the streams run full, so Penelope wept for her husband. Ulysses felt pity for his wife when he saw her crying, but he kept his own eyes as steady as if they were made of horn or iron.
Then Penelope said, “Friend, let me test you, to see whether this man really was my husband Ulysses. Tell me what clothes he wore, what kind of man he was, and who his companions were.”

Ulysses answered, “I remember that he wore a double cloak of wool, dyed sea-purple, fastened with a golden brooch. On the brooch was a dog holding a fawn by the throat, and both the dog and the fawn were wonderfully made. He also had a tunic, white and smooth, like the skin of a dry onion, which the women admired greatly. But I do not know whether someone had given him these things, for many people gave him gifts, and I did too: a sword and a tunic. He also had a herald with him, a man named Eurybates[1], who was older than he was, dark-skinned, round-shouldered, and curly-haired.”

When Penelope heard this, she wept even more, for she knew from these details that this man had truly seen her husband. “That is true,” she said. “Stranger, I gave him these clothes myself. I folded them with my own hands, and I gave him the jewel too. And now, alas, I will never see him again.”

But Ulysses answered, “No, wife of Ulysses, do not say that. Stop your mourning, for Ulysses is still alive. He is close by, in the land of the Thesprotians, and he is bringing many gifts with him. The king of that land told me so and showed me the gifts he had gathered. There were many of them and they were great, enough to make his house rich for ten generations. But Ulysses himself had gone to Dodona[2] when I was there, to ask Zeus whether he should come home openly or in secret, for the god’s oracle is there, in the middle of an oak tree. You can be sure, my lady, that Ulysses will come in this tenth year, just as the old moon wanes and the new one is born.”

Penelope said, “May your words come true, stranger! If they do, you will have plenty of kindness and many gifts from me. Yet I have a feeling in my heart that it will not happen. But now the maids will make up a bed for you with a mattress and blankets, so that you can sleep warm until morning comes. And they will wash your feet.”

But Ulysses said, “I have hated mattresses and blankets ever since I left the land of Crete. I will lie as I have lain for many nights, awake and waiting for the day. I take no pleasure in a bath either, and none of these maids will touch my feet. But if there is an old woman here with a faithful heart, I would let her touch my feet.”

Penelope said, “There is such a woman: the one who nursed my husband and took care of him, and carried him in her arms from the day his mother gave birth to him. She is weak with age now, but she will wash your feet.”
Then she said to the nurse, “Come now, wash this man, who is the same age as your master.”

The old woman covered her face with her hands and wept. She said, “I will gladly wash your feet, both for Penelope’s sake and for your own. Many strangers, worn out from traveling, have come here, but I never saw one who looked so much like Ulysses in his voice and his feet.”
Ulysses answered, “I have heard that before. People always said the two of us were very much alike.”

But when she had got the bath ready, Ulysses sat away from the hearth and turned his face to the darkness. He was afraid that when the old woman handled his leg, she would recognize a large scar on it, where a wild boar’s tusks had once torn him.
By this scar the old nurse realized that it was Ulysses himself. She said, “O Ulysses, my child, to think that I did not know you!”

She looked toward the Queen, meaning to tell her. But Ulysses put his hand on her throat and said softly, “Mother, do you want to kill me? I have come back after twenty years, and no one must know until I am ready to take my revenge.”

The old woman kept silent. After this Penelope talked with him again and told him her dreams. She had seen a flock of geese in her palace, and an eagle had killed them, and while she was mourning for the geese, a voice had said, “These geese are your suitors, and the eagle is your husband.”

Ulysses said that the dream was a good one. Then she told him that tomorrow she must make her choice, for she had promised to bring out the great bow of Ulysses. Whoever could string it most easily and shoot an arrow best at a target would be her husband.
Ulysses answered her, “That is good, my lady. Do not put off this test of the bow, for before any of them can draw the string, the great Ulysses will come and shoot at the target that is set up.”
After this Penelope went to sleep.
[1] Eu-ryb’-a-tes.
[2] Do-do’-na.

chapters.title: The Trial of the Bow
paragraphs: Ulysses made his bed in the gallery of the hall. He lay on a bull’s hide and covered himself with the fleeces of sheep that had been killed for the sacrifice and the feast, and the woman who kept the house threw a cloak over him.
But he could not sleep. His mind was full of thoughts, and he tossed from side to side, wondering how one man alone could kill so many suitors in his own hall.

Then Athene came down from Olympus and stood over his head, in the form of a woman. She said, “Are you still awake, man of so many troubles? Isn’t this your own house? Isn’t your wife inside, and your son, who is such a fine young man?”
Ulysses answered, “That is true, goddess. But I keep thinking how I, one man against so many, can kill the suitors in my hall.”

The goddess replied, “You have little faith. Some people put their trust in men, though men are weaker than the gods. Why won’t you trust in me? I am with you, and I will protect you to the end. Now go to sleep. Lying awake all night only wears you out.”
With these words she poured sleep over his eyes and went back to Olympus.

In the morning Ulysses woke up. He gathered the fleeces and put them on a seat in the hall, and he carried the bull’s hide outside. Then he lifted his hands to Zeus and prayed, “Father Zeus, if you have brought me to my own country willingly, then give me a sign.”

As soon as he spoke, Zeus thundered from Olympus, and Ulysses heard it and was glad. A woman at the mill also spoke a word of omen. Twelve women ground the wheat and barley there. Eleven of them had finished their work and were asleep, but this one, the weakest of them all, was still grinding. Now she stopped and said, “Father Zeus, this must be a sign, because you have thundered in a clear sky. Please let this be the last meal I ever grind for the suitors in the house of Ulysses!”
Next Telemachus came in and asked the nurse, “Have you given the guest food and bedding, or has he been left lying there with nothing?”

The nurse answered, “The stranger drank as much as he wanted and ate until he said he’d had enough. But he refused blankets and a mattress. He slept on a hide with sheepskins over him, and we threw a cloak over him as well.”
After that the swineherd arrived, leading three fat hogs, the best in the whole herd. He said, “Stranger, are these men treating you well?”
Ulysses answered, “May the gods pay them back for the insolent way they have treated me!”

Then Melanthius the goatherd came, bringing goats for the day’s feast. He spoke bitterly to Ulysses. “Are you still going to pester us with your begging, stranger? I think we won’t be rid of each other until we’ve settled it with our fists. Your begging is more than anyone can stand, and there are other feasts you could go to.”
But Ulysses did not say a word to him.

Last came Philoetius[1] the cattleherd, bringing a heifer for the suitors’ feast. He said to Ulysses, “I wish you happiness from now on, stranger! At the moment you are surrounded by sorrows. My eyes fill with tears when I look at you, because Ulysses may be wearing rags like yours and wandering among strangers, if he is still alive. And if he is dead, that is a great sorrow too. He put me in charge of his cattle, and they have grown beyond counting. No herds have ever multiplied more. Still, it grieves me that strangers keep devouring them in his hall. I would have run away long ago, because this is more than anyone can bear, except that I still hope to see Ulysses come home.”

Ulysses answered, “Cattleherd, you are a man with an understanding heart. Now listen to what I tell you. While you are still here, Ulysses will come home. You will see it with your own eyes, and you will see the suitors killed too.”

After a while the suitors arrived and sat down to the feast, as they always did. The servants brought Ulysses a full share, the same as the others, as Telemachus had ordered. When Ctesippus, a prince of Samos, saw this, he spoke up. He was a man who cared nothing for right or for the gods. “Is it fair that this fellow gets the same as us? Here, look at the gift I’ll give him.” He pulled a bullock’s foot out of a basket where it lay and threw it at Ulysses.
But Ulysses moved his head to the left and dodged it, and the foot flew on and hit the wall. Telemachus shouted furiously:—

“You are lucky, Ctesippus[2], that you did not hit this stranger. If you had, my spear would have gone right through you, and your father would have been holding a funeral feast for you instead of a wedding.”

Then Agelaus[3] said, “That is well said. Telemachus should not be wronged, and neither should this stranger. But on the other side, Telemachus must tell his mother to choose one of the suitors, whichever she likes, and marry him, so she stops wasting our time.”
Telemachus replied, “Very well. She may marry whomever she likes. But I will never send her out of my house against her will.”

After this, Penelope went to fetch the great bow of Ulysses. She took it down from the peg where it hung, still in its case, and sat down with it on her knees and wept over it. Then she got up and went to where the suitors were feasting in the hall. She brought the bow and also the quiver full of arrows. Standing by a pillar of the roof, she said:—

“Suitors, you who devour this house, here is a test of your skill. This is the bow of the great Ulysses. Whoever bends it most easily and shoots an arrow most easily through the holes in the heads of the twelve axes that Telemachus will set up, I will follow him and leave this house, which I will remember only in my dreams.”

Then she told Eumaeus to carry the bow and arrows to the suitors. The good swineherd wept when he saw his master’s bow, and Philoetius, the herdsman of the cattle, wept too, because he was a good man and loved the house of Ulysses.

Then Telemachus set up the axes in a row, each with its hole, and decided to try drawing the bow himself. He would even have done it, but Ulysses signaled to him not to. So he said, “I think I am too weak and young. You who are older should try first.”

First Leiodes[4], the priest, tried the bow. He was the only one among the suitors who hated their evil ways. But he could not move it. He only tired out his hands, which were soft and not used to hard work. He said, “I can’t bend this bow. Let someone else try. But I think it will bring grief and pain to many men today.”

Antinous was angry to hear such words. He told Melanthius to bring a roll of fat so they could rub the string with it and soften it. They greased the string, but they still could not bend the bow. All of them tried and failed, until only Antinous and Eurymachus were left, who were the bravest and strongest of them all.
Meanwhile the swineherd and the cattle herdsman had gone out into the yard. Ulysses followed them and said, “What would you do if Ulysses came back home? Would you fight for him or for the suitors?”
Both said they would fight for him.

Then Ulysses said, “It is I who have come back, in the twentieth year. I know you are both glad that I am home, and I know of no one else who is. If you help me bravely today, I will give you wives, and property, and houses close to mine. You will be like brothers and comrades to Telemachus. And as proof, look at this scar that the wild boar gave me.”

They wept for joy and kissed Ulysses, and he kissed them too. Then he told Eumaeus to bring him the bow once the suitors had finished trying it. He also told him to order the women to stay indoors and not come out, even if they heard the noise of battle. And he told Philoetius to lock the doors of the hall and tie them shut with a rope.

After this, Ulysses went back into the hall. Eurymachus had the bow in his hands and was trying to warm it by the fire. Then he tried to draw it, but could not. He groaned aloud and said, “How miserable I am! It is not only the loss of this marriage, since there are other women in Greece to woo. It is that we are so much weaker than the great Ulysses. That is a shame to tell.”
Antinous said, “Don’t say that. Today is a holy day of the god of archers, and that is why we couldn’t draw the bow. Tomorrow we will try again, after a sacrifice to Apollo.”
Everyone liked this idea, but Ulysses said, “Let me try this bow. I would like to know whether I still have the strength I had in the old days.”
At this the suitors were all furious, Antinous most of all. But Penelope said he should be allowed, and she promised the man great gifts if he could draw the bow.

Then Telemachus said, “Mother, the bow is mine to give or to refuse. No man can tell me no if I want this stranger to try it. But you go to your room with your maids, and let the men take care of these matters.”

He said this because he wanted her to leave the hall at once, knowing what was about to happen there. She was amazed to hear him speak with such authority, and she said nothing but left. Eumaeus started to carry the bow to Ulysses, and the suitors shouted roughly at him, but Telemachus made him go on. So he took the bow and gave it to his master. Then he went to Eurycleia and told her to shut the door of the women’s rooms and keep them inside, whatever they might hear.

Ulysses took the great bow in his hands and tested it to see whether it had been damaged, while the suitors looked on him with scorn. When he found that it had no flaw, he strung it easily, the way a minstrel fastens a string to his harp and tightens it to the right pitch. Holding the string in his right hand, he tested its tone, and it sounded as sweet as a swallow’s voice. Then he took an arrow from the quiver, laid the notch on the string and drew it, sitting just as he was. The arrow passed through every ring and stuck in the wall beyond. Then he said to Telemachus:—
“There is still a feast to be held before the sun goes down.”
And he nodded to Telemachus as a signal. At once the young man stood beside him, armed with spear, helmet and shield.
[1] Phi-loe’-ti-us.
[2] Cte-sip’-pus.
[3] A-ge-la’-us.
[4] Lei-o’-des.

chapters.title: The Slaying of the Suitors
paragraphs: Then Ulysses spoke to the suitors. “That task is finished. Now let me try another target.”

And he aimed his arrow at Antinous. The man was just lifting a cup to his lips and was not thinking of death. Who would have imagined that any man, even the mightiest of mortals, would dare such a deed when he was one against so many? The arrow went right through his neck. Blood gushed from his nostrils, and he dropped the cup and kicked the table away from him.

When the suitors saw him fall, they all leapt from their seats. But when they looked at the wall, there was no spear or shield there. They did not know whether the stranger had hit him by chance or on purpose. But Ulysses now told them who he was:—

“Dogs! You thought I would never come back! So you devoured my house, courted my wife while I was still alive, and feared neither the gods nor the judgment of men. Now sudden destruction has come upon you all.”

All the others trembled with fear, but Eurymachus spoke. “If you really are Ulysses of Ithaca, then you have spoken justly. You have been badly wronged, in your house and in your fields. But the man who was behind it all is lying here, Antinous. He did not want this marriage so much as he wanted to be king of this land, after destroying your house. But we will pay you back for everything we have devoured, twenty times over.”
But Ulysses said, “Don’t talk about paying me back. My hands will not stop killing until I have taken vengeance on every one of you.”

Then Eurymachus said to his companions, “This man will not hold back. He will shoot us all with his arrows from where he stands. Let us fight our way to the door and raise a cry in the city. Then this archer will soon have shot his last arrow.”

He rushed forward with his double-edged knife in his hand. But as he ran, Ulysses struck him in the chest with an arrow, and he fell on his face. When Amphinomus attacked, Telemachus killed him with his spear. He did not pull the spear out of the body, in case someone struck him unawares.
The young man hurried over to his father. “Should I go and get weapons for the two of us and for our helpers?”
“Yes,” said Ulysses, “and don’t waste time, or my arrows will run out.”

So Telemachus fetched four shields, four helmets and eight spears from the armory. He and the servants Eumaeus and Philoetius put on the armor. When his arrows were gone, Ulysses also put on a helmet and shield and took a mighty spear in each hand. But Melanthius the goatherd crept up to the armory and brought down twelve helmets and shields, and as many spears. When Ulysses saw the suitors arming themselves, he was very afraid, and he said to his son:—
“There is treachery here. It is one of the women, or maybe Melanthius the goatherd.”
Telemachus said, “That is my fault, father. I left the door of the room unlocked.”

Soon Eumaeus saw Melanthius sneaking up to the room again, and he followed, with Philoetius beside him. They caught him just as he was taking a helmet in one hand and a shield in the other. They tied his hands and feet and hoisted him up by a rope to the beams of the ceiling.

Then the two men went back to the hall, and Athene came there too, in the shape of Mentor. But she wanted to test the courage of Ulysses and his son further, so she did not help them yet. Instead she changed her shape and sat on the roof beam like a swallow.
Then Agelaus cried out, “Friends, Mentor is gone, and he is not helping them. Let’s not throw our spears at random, but let six of us attack together. Maybe we can defeat them.”

They threw their spears, but Athene turned them aside, one into the pillar, another into the door and another into the wall. Ulysses, Telemachus and the two herdsmen each killed a man, and then did it again, and again. Only Amphimedon[1] wounded Telemachus, and Ctesippus grazed the shoulder of Eumaeus. But Telemachus struck Amphimedon down, and the cattle herdsman killed Ctesippus, saying, “Take this, for the ox-foot you gave to our guest.” All the while Athene waved her flaming shield from above, and the suitors fell like birds scattered and torn by eagles.

Then Leiodes, the priest, begged Ulysses for mercy. “I never did any harm in this house,” he said, “and I tried to stop the others, but they wouldn’t listen. All I ever did was serve at the altar. Please don’t kill me.”
Ulysses answered him, “It is enough that you served at the altar of these men, and that you wanted to marry my wife.”

And he killed him. But he spared Phemius, the minstrel, who had sung for the suitors in the hall only because they forced him, not because he wished to. He spared Medon, the herald, too, and told them both to go out into the yard. There they sat, clinging to the altar and glancing around in fear, because they still thought they would die.

So the slaughter of the suitors was over. Now Ulysses ordered the hall to be cleaned, the benches and tables washed with water, and the whole place purified with sulphur. When that was done, he said, Eurycleia, the nurse, should go to Penelope and tell her that her husband had truly come home.
[1] Am- phim’-e-don.

chapters.title: The End of the Wandering
paragraphs: Eurycleia hurried to her mistress’s room with the happy news. In her great joy she rushed so fast that her feet stumbled over each other. She stood by Penelope’s head and said, “Wake up, dear child, and see with your own eyes what you have longed for all this time. Ulysses has come back, and he has killed the men who were eating up his wealth!”

But Penelope answered, “Dear nurse, the gods must have taken away your good sense. They can turn a wise person into a fool, and they can make a simple person wise. Why do you mock me and wake me from my sleep, the sweetest I have had since the day Ulysses sailed for Troy, that hateful city? Go back to the women’s rooms! If any other maid had woken me like this, I would have sent her away with a sharp scolding. But your old age protects you.”

The nurse said, “I’m not mocking you, dear child. Ulysses really is here. He is the stranger who was treated so shamefully. Telemachus knew who he was long ago, but he kept it secret so they could take revenge on the suitors.”

Then Penelope was overjoyed. She jumped out of bed, threw her arms around the old woman’s neck, and wept. “Tell me the truth,” she said. “Has he really come home and killed the suitors, one man against so many?”

The nurse replied, “I don’t know how it was done. I only heard the groans of the men being killed. We women sat in our room in amazement until your son called me. Then I found Ulysses standing among the dead, who lay piled on top of one another. You would have been glad to see him, child. He looked like a lion, covered in blood from the labor of the fight. Now the suitors lie in a heap, and he is purifying his house with sulphur. Come, so that you can put an end to all the sorrow you have suffered, because what you wished for has come true. Your husband is home, and he has fully punished these wicked men.”

But Penelope said, “Dear nurse, don’t be too bold in your joy. You know how gladly I would see him. But this is not he. One of the gods killed the suitors, angry at their insolence and their wrongdoing. Ulysses himself is dead.”

Then the nurse said, “What are you saying? That your husband will never return, when he is already in his own house? You are truly slow to believe. Here is a clear proof that I saw with my own eyes: the scar from the wound a wild boar gave him with its tusk long ago. I saw it when I washed his feet. I wanted to tell you, but he put his hand over my mouth and, in his wisdom, wouldn’t let me speak.”
Penelope answered her, “It is hard for you to understand the plans of the gods. Still, I will go to my son, so that I can see the dead suitors and the man who killed them.”

So she went down and sat in the dim light by the opposite wall, while Ulysses sat by a pillar with his eyes on the ground, waiting for his wife to speak to him. But she was deeply confused. One moment she seemed to know him, and the next she didn’t, because he had not let the women dress him in fresh clothes.
Telemachus said, “Mother, cruel mother, why do you sit apart from my father and not speak to him? Your heart must be harder than stone.”

But Ulysses said, “Leave her alone, Telemachus. In good time your mother will know what is true. For now, let us hide this slaughter for a while, so that the friends of these men don’t come looking for revenge against us. So let there be music and dancing in the hall. Then people will say, ‘This is the Queen’s wedding, and the palace is full of joy,’ and they won’t know the truth.”

So the minstrel played and the women danced. Meanwhile Ulysses went to bathe and put on fine clothes, and Athene made him look handsome and young. He came back to the hall and sat down again, across from his wife, and said:—
“Lady, the gods have made your heart harder than that of any other woman. Would any other wife stay away from her husband when he comes back after twenty years?”

When she still doubted, he spoke again. “Listen, Penelope, and know that it really is I. I will tell you how my bed was made. In the inner court there grew an olive tree, with a trunk as thick as a pillar. I built the bedroom around it, roofed it over, and put doors on it. Then I trimmed the branches off the olive and shaped the trunk into the bedpost. Starting from that, I built the bed itself until it was finished, inlaying it with gold, silver, and ivory. Inside I stretched a strap of ox-hide dyed purple. Whether the bed is still in its place, or whether someone has moved it—and it would be no easy thing to move—I don’t know. But that is how I made it long ago.”

Then Penelope knew that he was truly her husband. She ran to him, threw her arms around him, and kissed him. “Forgive me, my lord, for being slow to know you,” she said. “I was always afraid that someone would trick me by claiming to be my husband. But now I know that you are he and no one else.”
They cried in each other’s arms and kissed again and again. That was how Ulysses finally came home, after twenty years away.

chapters.title: The Triumph of Ulysses
paragraphs: Meanwhile Ulysses left his palace and went to the house of Laertes, out in the fields. The old man lived there, looked after by a woman from Sicily. Ulysses spoke to his son and the shepherds. “Go into the house and prepare a meal of pork, as tasty as you can make it,” he said. “I want to test my father and see whether he will know me. He may well have forgotten me, since I’ve been away so long.”

So Ulysses spoke, and he also gave his weapons to the men to look after. They went into the house, and Ulysses went to the orchard to look for his father. He did not find Dolius[1], Laertes’ steward, or any of the servants or Dolius’s sons, because they had gone to build a fence around the field. He found only the old man, busy digging around a tree. His tunic was filthy and patched with stitches. He wore ox-hide wraps on his legs to protect them from thorns, gloves on his hands, and a dog-skin cap on his head. When Ulysses saw how worn out with age and sorrow his father looked, he stood under a pear tree and wept. For a while he debated with himself whether to kiss and embrace his father, make himself known, and tell him he had come home, or whether to question him first and learn everything he wanted to know. He decided it was better to question him first. So he went up to the old man, who was digging around a tree with his head bent down.

Then Ulysses said, “Old man, you certainly know how to take care of an orchard. Not a fig, vine, olive, or pear tree can thrive in a garden without care. But let me say one more thing, and don’t be angry when you hear it. Your garden is well tended, but you yourself are in a sorry state. Old age weighs heavily on you, and your clothes are filthy. Yet it can’t be because you are lazy that your master treats you this way. You don’t look at all like a slave, either, because your face and bearing are those of a king. A man like you should be able to wash, sit down to a meal, and sleep in comfort, because that is the right of old age. But tell me honestly, whose servant are you? Whose orchard do you tend? And tell me this too: is this really the land of Ithaca, where I have come? A man I met on my way here told me so, but he seemed rather simple-minded. He wouldn’t listen to me, and he wouldn’t tell me whether a friend of mine who lives here is alive or dead. I welcomed that friend into my house long ago, and no guest was ever dearer to me. He told me he was the son of Laertes and came from the land of Ithaca.”

Laertes answered him, weeping as he spoke. “You can be sure, stranger, that you have come to the land you asked about. But wicked and violent men hold it now. If you had found the son of Laertes here, he would have sent you away with many gifts. But tell me honestly, was it long ago that you welcomed him into your house? He is my son, unhappy man that I am. Either he has drowned in the sea and the fish have eaten him, or wild beasts and birds have devoured him on land. Neither his father nor his mother, nor his wife Penelope, the most prudent of women, could mourn over him or lay him out for burial. But tell me, who are you? Where is your city, and who are your parents? Did your own ship bring you here, with your companions, or did you come as a trader on someone else’s ship?”

Then Ulysses said, “I will tell you all this truthfully. My name is Eperitus.[2] It was the doing of the gods that I came here from the land of Sicily, and not by my own choice. My ship is moored nearby. As for Ulysses, it is now the fifth year since he left me. And yet the omens were good when he set out on his journey, so that we both rejoiced, thinking that he would travel safely and that we would be friends to each other in the time to come.”

So Ulysses spoke, and when his father, the old man, heard these words, great grief came over him. He scooped up dust in both hands and poured it over his white hair. Ulysses’ heart was stirred when he saw this, and he was close to tears as he looked at his father. Then he threw his arms around him, kissed him, and said, “Father, here I am, the son you are weeping for. Look! I have come back to my own country after twenty years, and I have taken revenge on the men who wanted to marry my wife. I have killed them all.”
The old man answered him, “If you are really my son Ulysses, give me some clear sign so that I can know you.”

Then Ulysses said, “Look at this scar on my thigh, where the wild boar wounded me on Mount Parnassus.[3] You and my mother sent me to my grandfather, and I was hurt on the hunt. Here is another sign, too. I will tell you which of the orchard trees you gave me long ago, when I was a boy walking with you and asking their names. You gave me thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees, and forty fig trees. You also promised me fifty rows of vines, to be mine when the grapes ripened.”

The old man’s heart was moved, and his knees gave way, because he knew the signs were true. He threw his arms around his son, and his spirit revived. He said, “Now I know there are gods in heaven, since I hear that these wicked men have been punished for their wrongdoing. Still, I fear that their families will stir up the men of Ithaca and the islands around us against us.”
Then Ulysses said, “Don’t trouble yourself with that, Father. Let’s go to the house instead. Telemachus is there with Eumaeus and the cowherd, and they have prepared everything so that we can eat.”

So they went to the house and found Telemachus and his companions carving the meat for the dinner and mixing the wine. Then the woman from Sicily bathed the old man Laertes, rubbed him with oil, and dressed him in a fine cloak. Athene also stood beside him and made him taller and stronger than before. His son marveled to see him, so handsome was he, like the gods who live forever. He said to him, “Father, surely one of the immortal gods has made you tall and handsome!”

Laertes replied, “If only, by God, I had stood beside you yesterday and taken revenge on the suitors with the strength I had in my younger days! I would have killed many a man with my spear, and you would have been proud.”

So they talked together. When dinner was ready, they sat down to eat. Then old Dolius came in from his work with his sons, since the Sicilian woman, who was their mother, had called them. When they saw Ulysses, they stood still, amazed and speechless. Ulysses said to them, “Old man, stop staring and sit down to eat. We have been ready for our meal, and we have waited a long time for you.”

Then Dolius ran to him with both hands outstretched, took Ulysses’ hand, and kissed it on the wrist. He said, “We are so glad you’ve come, because we never expected you. It must be the gods who brought you back. May all go well with you. But tell me, does Queen Penelope know you’re here, or should I send a messenger to tell her?”
“She knows,” said Ulysses. Then the old man sat down to eat, and his sons after him, once they had greeted Ulysses.

Meanwhile the news that the suitors had been killed spread through the city. The families of the dead men came to the house of Ulysses, weeping and groaning, and carried the bodies away and buried them. The men who came from other lands they loaded onto ships, to be taken home and laid in their fathers’ tombs. When this was done, the people gathered in the marketplace. Eupeithes[4] stood up before them, deeply troubled in his heart for his son Antinous, the first of the suitors whom Ulysses had killed. He stood in the middle of the crowd and said, “This man has done terrible harm to our land. First he led many brave comrades away to Troy, and he lost them all, and their ships too. Now he has come back and killed the princes of our people. It would be a disgrace to us, now and for all the generations to come, if we did not take revenge on the men who killed our sons and our brothers. I tell you, I don’t want to go on living if they go unpunished. Come, let’s hurry, before they cross the sea and escape.”

Eupeithes wept as he spoke, and when the people heard him, they felt sorry for him. But Medon the herald stood up in the assembly and said, “Listen to me, men of Ithaca! Ulysses did not do all this without help from the gods who live forever. I saw it with my own eyes: one of the gods stood beside Ulysses, looking just like Prince Mentor. A god stood by Ulysses and gave him strength, and another was among the suitors, throwing them into confusion so that they fell.”

After Medon the herald had spoken, Alitherses[5] the seer stood up. He knew everything that had happened and everything that was still to come. He said, “Men of Ithaca, all this has come about because of your own foolishness. You would not listen to me, or to Mentor, and you would not hold your sons back from their folly. They did great wrong, wasting the property of a brave man and courting his wife, because they did not believe he would ever return. Now listen to me, or something even worse will happen to you.”

Then some of the men got up and hurried away, and they were the larger part of the crowd. But the others stayed where they were, because they did not like the advice of Medon and the seer and preferred what Eupeithes had said. So they put on their armor and marched toward the city, with Eupeithes at their head.
Then Athene spoke to Zeus. “Tell me, my father, what is in your mind. Do you want war or friendship between these two sides?”

Zeus answered her, “Why do you ask me this? Wasn’t it your own plan that Ulysses should kill the suitors in his palace? Arrange it however you like. But in the end let there be peace and friendship, so that Ulysses can prosper in the land and the people can live happily around him.”
Then Athene left and came down to the land of Ithaca.
When Ulysses and the men sitting with him had finished eating and drinking, the King said, “Someone go out and see whether those men are close by.”
So the son of Dolius went out. Standing on the threshold, he saw the men coming and cried, “They are almost here! Let’s arm ourselves as fast as we can.”

So they put on their armor. With Ulysses were Telemachus, Eumaeus and the keeper of the herds. Six sons of Dolius stood with him too, and the two old men as well, Laertes and Dolius, though their hair was white with age. As they left the house, Athene came up to them, looking and sounding like Prince Mentor. Ulysses was glad at heart when he saw her, and he said to Telemachus, “I know you well, my son. You will fight bravely and bring no dishonor on the house of your fathers, who have always been famous in this land for courage and manliness.”
Telemachus answered, “Father, you will see that for yourself, if you wish.”
Laertes was glad at heart too, and he said, “What a happy day this is, when my son and my grandson are competing with each other in bravery.”
Then Athene went up to the old man and said, “Laertes, first pray to Athene and to Father Zeus, and then throw your spear.”

With these words she breathed great strength into his heart. After he had prayed, he threw his spear and struck Eupeithes through the helmet, and Eupeithes fell dead on the ground. Then Ulysses and his son charged the men of Ithaca with swords and two-handed spears. They would surely have killed every one of them, but Athene cried out loudly, “Stop fighting, men of Ithaca! This battle is too hard for you.”

The men were terrified when they heard her voice. They threw their weapons on the ground and ran, hoping to escape to the city. When Ulysses was about to chase after them, Zeus hurled a thunderbolt from heaven, and it landed right in front of Athene’s feet. Then Athene cried, “Stop fighting, son of Laertes, or Zeus will be angry with you.”
Ulysses stopped fighting, and Zeus and Athene brought peace between the King and the people of Ithaca.
